Nearly three decades after Tupac Shakur was fatally shot in Las Vegas, the long-running murder case has finally produced its first criminal conviction. On August 31, 2026, a Las Vegas jury found Duane "Keffe D" Davis guilty of first-degree murder in connection with Shakur's 1996 killing. The jury reached its verdict in less than three hours, bringing a major development to one of the most closely watched unsolved cases in music history.

Davis, 63, was convicted of murder with the use of a deadly weapon. He could face a life sentence, with sentencing scheduled for October 13, and he has indicated that he intends to appeal the conviction.

The night Tupac Shakur was shot

The events began on September 7, 1996, after a Mike Tyson boxing match at the MGM Grand in Las Vegas. Shakur was travelling in a BMW driven by Death Row Records co-founder Marion "Suge" Knight when a confrontation broke out at the casino. Shakur and members of his entourage attacked Orlando "Baby Lane" Anderson, who was Davis's nephew and associated with the South Side Compton Crips.

Later that night, Shakur and Knight were stopped at a red light near the Las Vegas Strip. A white Cadillac pulled alongside their vehicle and gunfire erupted. Shakur was struck multiple times, and Knight was also wounded but survived. Shakur was taken to hospital, where he died six days later on September 13, 1996, at the age of 25. For years, no one was charged.

Who is Duane "Keffe D" Davis?

Davis was a former leader and influential figure within the South Side Compton Crips. Unlike the person prosecutors believe fired the fatal shots, Davis was not accused of being the gunman. Instead, prosecutors argued that he helped organise the attack, obtained the firearm, and coordinated the group that went looking for Shakur and Knight after the MGM Grand confrontation.

Under Nevada law, a person can be held criminally responsible for murder even if they did not personally pull the trigger, when their involvement makes them legally responsible for the killing. That distinction became central to the trial.

The prosecution's case

Perhaps the most unusual aspect of the prosecution's case was how heavily it relied on Davis's own words. Over the years, Davis had repeatedly spoken publicly about the shooting, discussing the events in interviews, documentaries, and his 2019 memoir, Compton Street Legend. Prosecutors also presented recordings of conversations with investigators.

Although some details in Davis's accounts changed over time, prosecutors argued that one crucial element remained consistent, Davis repeatedly placed himself inside the white Cadillac involved in the shooting. Prosecutors portrayed Davis as the person who organised the retaliation after the assault on Anderson, and Chief Deputy District Attorney Binu Palal argued that Davis obtained a gun, assembled the group, and went searching for Shakur and Knight. The prosecution maintained that the shooting was not a spontaneous confrontation but the result of a deliberate plan, and ultimately called 24 witnesses during the trial, while the defence called three.

The defence challenged Davis's own story

Davis's defence did not dispute that he had spoken about the killing over the years. Instead, his lawyers questioned whether those statements were reliable enough to establish his guilt beyond a reasonable doubt. Defence attorney Michael Sanft pointed to the lack of direct physical evidence placing Davis at the Las Vegas shooting scene, including the absence of surveillance footage or phone records connecting him to the location that night.

The defence also argued that Davis had reasons to exaggerate his involvement, particularly because he had discussed the killing publicly and profited from his notoriety. But prosecutors countered that although Davis's accounts evolved, their central elements remained remarkably consistent.

Why it took almost 30 years

The investigation remained stalled for decades. Shakur's death became intertwined with the larger East Coast to West Coast hip-hop rivalry of the 1990s, generating countless theories about who was responsible and why, yet investigators were unable to bring a murder charge for years.

Davis eventually became increasingly public about his version of events, and those statements ultimately became a major part of the evidence used against him. He was arrested and charged in 2023, becoming the only person ever formally charged in connection with Shakur's murder. The other men prosecutors identified as being inside the Cadillac are now dead, leaving Davis as the only surviving person prosecutors say was in the vehicle.

A historic verdict for hip-hop

The conviction represents the first criminal resolution in Tupac Shakur's murder case. For nearly 30 years, the unanswered question surrounding Shakur's death became part of his mythology, discussed in music, documentaries, books, and countless theories, while his influence continued to grow long after his death.

Shakur remains one of the most influential artists in hip-hop history. His music addressed poverty, racism, inequality, violence, identity, and the realities of life in America, helping transform him from a successful rapper into a cultural figure whose work continues to influence new generations. His death at 25 made his legacy even more enduring.

What happens now?

Davis remains in custody without bail while awaiting sentencing. He could receive a life sentence, and he has already indicated that he plans to appeal the verdict. The conviction does not answer every question surrounding the killing, prosecutors did not argue that Davis personally fired the fatal shots, and the precise identity of the gunman remains part of the historical record surrounding the case.

But legally, the verdict marks a significant turning point. After nearly three decades of investigation, speculation, and uncertainty, a jury has now determined that Duane "Keffe D" Davis was criminally responsible for Tupac Shakur's murder. For one of hip-hop's most enduring mysteries, the story that began with a shooting on a Las Vegas street in 1996 has finally reached its first courtroom conclusion.

Dubai is hosting the 22nd edition of the International Property Show (IPS) 2026, running September 7 to 9 at the Dubai World Trade Centre. The exhibition brings together property developers, investors, brokers, architects, technology companies, and other professionals from across the real estate industry.

It gives developers a platform to showcase residential, commercial, and mixed-use projects, while giving investors and prospective buyers an opportunity to explore property opportunities in Dubai and international markets. More than 300 exhibitors are expected to participate, representing different parts of the real estate ecosystem.

What is the International Property Show?

The International Property Show is one of Dubai's major real estate exhibitions, bringing together developers, brokers, investors, financial institutions, architects, proptech companies, and other property-sector professionals. The event covers residential and commercial property, off-plan developments, international property investment, real estate brokerage and advisory, architecture and construction, property technology, investment and financing, and real estate market intelligence.

For buyers, the exhibition can provide an opportunity to speak directly with developers and compare projects in one location.

Major Dubai developers at IPS 2026

A number of prominent developers are participating in IPS 2026, including Azizi Properties, Binghatti, Danube Properties, Fakhruddin Properties, SanZen, and Union Properties. Their participation reflects the continued activity across Dubai's residential and commercial property market, with developments ranging from new residential communities to mixed-use projects and investment-focused properties.

For prospective buyers, meeting developers directly can also make it easier to ask questions about payment plans, construction progress, handover dates, and ongoing ownership costs.

Why IPS 2026 matters for Dubai's property market

Dubai's real estate market has continued to attract international investors, developers, and property professionals, while new projects are reshaping communities across the emirate. IPS brings many of these participants together under one roof, which makes the exhibition relevant not only to people looking to purchase property, but also to professionals involved in development, architecture, financing, marketing, technology, and property management.

For international investors in particular, the event provides an opportunity to learn more about Dubai's property market while comparing different developers and locations.

What should buyers look for?

A property exhibition can be a useful starting point for research, but buyers should avoid making decisions based solely on promotional material or projected investment returns. Before reserving a property, prospective buyers should investigate a handful of things.

Check developer and project registration, confirming whether the developer and project are properly registered with the relevant Dubai authorities, including the Dubai Land Department and RERA where applicable. Understand the complete payment plan, including the booking amount, instalments, post-handover payments, and any penalties for late payments. Ask for the latest construction status and expected handover date rather than relying only on launch presentations or promotional material. Factor in recurring ownership costs such as service charges, maintenance, and other community-related expenses.

For off-plan purchases specifically, buyers should understand the project's escrow arrangements and the contractual terms governing payments. And projected rental yields and future capital appreciation are not guaranteed, so it's worth comparing a developer's projections against actual rental and sales data from comparable properties before relying on them.

IPS 2026 is more than a property exhibition

For developers, IPS provides a platform to launch and promote projects to potential buyers and investors. For investors, it can be an opportunity to compare multiple developments, speak directly with industry professionals, and gather information about different areas of Dubai. And for the wider property industry, the event brings together the companies and professionals responsible for developing, financing, designing, marketing, and managing real estate.

A useful opportunity for property research

With hundreds of exhibitors and major developers participating, IPS 2026 offers visitors a concentrated look at Dubai's evolving real estate landscape. However, the most valuable approach for prospective buyers is to treat the exhibition as a research opportunity rather than a reason to make an immediate purchase.

Compare developments, request documentation, investigate the developer's track record, and understand the complete cost of ownership before committing to a property. Dubai's property market continues to evolve rapidly, and exhibitions such as IPS provide a window into the developments and investment opportunities shaping the city's next phase of growth.

Dubai is heading into a new outdoor season, with several of the city's most popular attractions preparing to reopen after the summer, while some major landmarks remain temporarily closed for renovations and major upgrades. From Global Village and Dubai Safari Park returning in October 2026 to the Museum of the Future's planned 2027 relaunch and the Burj Al Arab's expected reopening in October 2027, the coming months will bring a mix of seasonal returns and major transformations.

Some dates have been confirmed, while others remain estimates. Visitors should check official attraction and hotel websites before making bookings.

Global Village returns in October

Global Village is expected to return in October 2026 for its 31st season, with the season expected to continue through May 2027. The exact opening date has not yet been announced. In recent years, Global Village has generally opened around the middle of October, meaning October 14 or October 21 could be possible dates, though these remain estimates until officially confirmed.

The seasonal attraction brings together international pavilions, food outlets, shopping, live entertainment, rides, and family activities. Its return is also one of the clearest signs that Dubai's outdoor season is beginning after the hottest months of the year.

Dubai Safari Park expected to reopen

Dubai Safari Park is also expected to begin its eighth season in October 2026. The park traditionally closes during the summer before reopening as temperatures become more comfortable for outdoor activities. The attraction features wildlife areas, safari experiences, and educational programmes, making it particularly popular with families.

While October has been identified as the expected reopening month, visitors should wait for the official opening date before planning a visit.

Dubai Miracle Garden could return in late September

Dubai Miracle Garden is expected to return for its 15th season around late September or early October 2026. An official reopening date had not been announced at the time of writing. The previous season opened on September 29, 2025, which makes a similar timeframe possible, but that should not be treated as a confirmed date.

The attraction is known for its enormous floral installations, themed displays, and colourful walking routes. Like other major outdoor attractions, it operates primarily during Dubai's cooler months.

Museum of the Future closes for a major revamp

While outdoor attractions prepare to return, one of Dubai's most recognisable landmarks is temporarily going in the opposite direction. The Museum of the Future's current exhibitions will close to the public on September 15, 2026, with the venue shutting from September 16 to undergo a major overhaul of its exhibitions and visitor experiences.

The existing experiences are expected to be replaced with a new generation of immersive and interactive exhibitions focused on technology, science, design, and future-oriented ideas, developed with input from more than 1,000 contributors from around the world. The museum is expected to return during the first quarter of 2027, timed to coincide with its fifth anniversary and featuring a new flagship experience called Mission 2071, though an exact reopening date has not yet been announced.

Burj Al Arab set for a major transformation

Another iconic Dubai landmark undergoing extensive work is the Burj Al Arab. The luxury hotel closed in April 2026 for an approximately 18-month programme of interior upgrades, restoration, and preservation work, led by French interior architect Tristan Auer.

The hotel is currently expected to reopen in October 2027, although a specific date has not been confirmed. The project is designed to preserve the hotel's distinctive interiors while updating elements of the guest experience. As one of Dubai's most recognisable symbols of luxury hospitality, the reopening is likely to attract considerable attention from both the tourism industry and international visitors.

Other Dubai hotel reopenings

Several other prominent hotels are also expected to return following renovation or upgrade programmes.

Hotel Expected reopening
St. Regis Dubai, The Palm From September 1, 2026
Armani Hotel Dubai Q4 2026
Park Hyatt Dubai November 2026
Burj Al Arab October 2027

These dates should be treated as reported targets rather than guaranteed opening dates, as renovation schedules can change.

Dubai's outdoor season returns in stages

Dubai's seasonal calendar doesn't switch from summer to winter overnight. Indoor attractions, shopping destinations, and many hotels continue operating throughout the hotter months, while outdoor attractions gradually return as temperatures become more comfortable. Late September and October are therefore likely to be particularly active for Dubai's outdoor attractions.

Global Village and Dubai Safari Park are expected back in October, while Miracle Garden could return around the same period. At the same time, major landmarks such as the Museum of the Future and Burj Al Arab are undergoing transformations that will extend into 2027.

What visitors should know

If you're planning activities for the coming months, it's worth checking the official website of each attraction before purchasing tickets. Global Village is expected to return in October 2026, with an exact date still pending, and Dubai Safari Park is expected on a similar timeline. Miracle Garden could return in late September or early October, though its date is also pending. The Museum of the Future closes to the public on September 15, 2026, with the venue shutting the following day for redevelopment, and the Burj Al Arab is expected to reopen in October 2027. Hotel reopening dates in particular can change depending on renovation progress.

The result is an interesting transition for Dubai, the city's outdoor attractions are preparing to come back just as some of its most recognisable landmarks are being redesigned for the future. For residents and visitors, the next few months should bring plenty of familiar destinations returning alongside a new generation of experiences waiting to emerge in 2027.

Apple has confirmed the UAE launch of the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max. Pre-orders open on September 12, with both models reaching stores on September 18. The new foldable iPhone Duo will follow on October 23.

Apple's newest iPhone generation is officially heading to the UAE, and buyers in Dubai won't have to wait behind the US or other major markets. The UAE is included in Apple's first wave of countries for the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max, with pre-orders beginning on Saturday, September 12, 2026, followed by full retail availability on Friday, September 18. That means customers in Dubai and across the Emirates can purchase the new Pro models from Apple and participating retailers from September 18.

iPhone 18 Pro UAE release date

Here are the dates UAE buyers need to know.

UAE date
iPhone 18 Pro pre-orders September 12, 2026 at 4:00 PM
iPhone 18 Pro Max pre-orders September 12, 2026 at 4:00 PM
iPhone 18 Pro retail availability September 18, 2026
iPhone 18 Pro Max retail availability September 18, 2026
iPhone Duo pre-orders October 16, 2026 at 4:00 PM
iPhone Duo availability October 23, 2026

Apple's UAE website specifically lists 4:00 PM local time for both the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone Duo pre-order windows.

How much will the iPhone 18 Pro cost in the UAE?

Apple has published official UAE pricing. The iPhone 18 Pro starts at AED 5,099, while the larger iPhone 18 Pro Max starts at AED 5,499. Both phones are available with 256GB, 512GB, 1TB, and 2TB storage options, in black, silver, glacier, and an all-new burgundy finish. Higher-capacity configurations rise substantially, with the top 2TB configuration listed at more than AED 10,000 on Apple's UAE store.

What about the iPhone Duo?

UAE customers will have to wait a little longer for Apple's most unusual new iPhone. Apple has confirmed the iPhone Duo will be available in the UAE, with pre-orders beginning at 4:00 PM on October 16 and availability starting October 23. The Duo starts from AED 8,499, considerably more expensive than the iPhone 18 Pro.

The Duo introduces the largest display Apple has ever put on an iPhone. Closed, it has a 5.4-inch outer screen and is roughly passport-sized. Opened, it reveals a 7.6-inch inner display, the largest screen Apple has offered on an iPhone. The folding design is more than a way to fit a bigger screen in a pocket, users can prop the phone up for video calls or photos without a stand, run apps across the larger display, and use the outer screen as a preview when photographing someone. There's even a feature called Kid Cue, which displays Peanuts animations on the outer screen to encourage children to look toward the camera, one of several examples of Apple building software specifically around the two-screen format. The Duo is available in Star White and Night Sky.

So if you're choosing between Apple's new flagship models, the UAE launch schedule is effectively split into two waves, September 18 for the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max, and October 23 for the iPhone Duo.

UAE iPhone 18 models will be eSIM-only

There's another important change UAE buyers should know about. The iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max sold in the UAE, along with the iPhone Duo, are eSIM-only, meaning the physical SIM tray has been removed. Apple says removing the physical SIM hardware creates additional internal space for the battery. The UAE joins markets including Bahrain, Kuwait, Oman, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, Japan, Canada, and the United States in receiving these eSIM-only models.

For UAE users, both e& and du support eSIM, according to Apple's regional information. Anyone moving from an older physical-SIM iPhone should make sure their mobile number is transferred to an eSIM when upgrading.

What's new with the iPhone 18 Pro?

The headline camera upgrade this year is Apple's new 48MP Fusion Main camera with variable aperture. Instead of relying entirely on computational photography, the physical aperture can change to control incoming light and depth of field, giving users more control over portraits, low-light photos, and background blur. Apple is also adding more manual Pro controls to the Camera app, and both models get a smaller Dynamic Island.

Inside is Apple's new A20 Pro chip, manufactured using a 2-nanometre process and paired with a next-generation thermal system for sustained performance. Apple is also introducing its C2 cellular modem and N1 wireless networking chip. Battery life reaches up to 45 hours of video playback on the iPhone 18 Pro Max, the longest of the pair, according to Apple.

Where can you buy it in Dubai?

Apple's UAE online store will begin accepting pre-orders at 4:00 PM on September 12, with confirmed general availability from September 18. Given the demand normally surrounding new flagship iPhones, buyers looking for a particular colour or storage configuration may want to order during the pre-order window rather than relying on launch-day stock.

The important dates

For Dubai buyers, the answer is straightforward. The iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max arrive in the UAE on September 18, 2026, with pre-orders opening six days earlier on September 12. Those waiting for Apple's first foldable will need another month, the iPhone Duo launches in the UAE on October 23, starting from AED 8,499.

For once, UAE customers aren't waiting for a later international rollout. Dubai is part of Apple's opening wave.

Dubai is about to gain something it has never had before, a place on a national passenger railway. On September 30, Etihad Rail's Dubai station opens at Al Yalayis, connecting the city to a rail network that is beginning to redraw how people move between the Emirates.

For decades, travelling between the UAE's cities has largely meant getting into a car, taking a taxi or boarding an intercity bus. Dubai has built one of the region's most extensive urban public transport systems, but once a journey crossed the emirate's boundary, the car remained dominant.

That begins to change on September 30, 2026.

Passenger rail has already started in the UAE

Technically, the railway era has already begun.

At 5:34am on June 30, Etihad Rail's first scheduled passenger service departed Fujairah for Abu Dhabi. It arrived at Mohammed Bin Zayed City at 7:19am, completing the journey in one hour and 45 minutes. It was the first scheduled national passenger rail service in the UAE.

That initial route has effectively served as the introductory phase before the wider rollout, and demand has been strong. Etihad Rail reported more than 70,000 tickets sold within five weeks of launch, with passengers booking an average of 12 days ahead and several services selling out entirely. The operator said demand was coming from families, business travellers, schools and leisure passengers.

September 30 is the next significant date. It is when the railway reaches Dubai, opening alongside Al Dhaid station in Sharjah.

Where is the Etihad Rail station in Dubai?

Dubai's passenger station, known as Al Yalayis station, sits inside Jumeirah Golf Estates, directly along Sheikh Mohammed Bin Zayed Road, placing it close to the existing Dubai Metro Red Line corridor.

This matters because the usefulness of an intercity railway depends heavily on what happens after passengers step off the train. Rather than functioning as an isolated station on Dubai's outskirts, the location is intended to integrate with the city's wider transport network. The Etihad Rail station sits roughly four minutes from the existing Jumeirah Golf Estates Metro station, and a footbridge connecting the two is currently under construction.

That creates the possibility of journeys that previously required a car becoming predominantly public transport. A passenger arriving in Dubai could continue by Metro towards areas including Dubai Marina, JLT, Downtown Dubai, Business Bay or Dubai International Airport through the wider Metro network.

The significance isn't simply having a railway station. It is connecting national rail with local transport, and once the two are linked, the Dubai to Abu Dhabi journey by rail is expected to take around 57 minutes.


Why September 30 matters for Dubai

Dubai already has Metro, Tram, buses, taxis and an expanding network of cycling and pedestrian infrastructure.

Etihad Rail fills a different gap.

The Metro moves people around Dubai. Etihad Rail is designed to move people between the Emirates. That distinction could gradually change how residents think about distance.

Living in one emirate and working in another is already normal for many UAE residents. But those journeys are largely dictated by traffic conditions. Rail introduces something different, predictability. Instead of asking how congested Sheikh Zayed Road or another highway might be at a particular time, passengers can plan around a timetable.

Etihad Rail itself describes passenger rail as an additional travel choice rather than a replacement for existing transport, with reliability and predictable inter-emirate movement among its central aims.


The railway could make the UAE feel smaller

This may eventually be the most important consequence.

The UAE is geographically compact, yet the way its cities have developed can make them feel more separated than the map suggests. Dubai, Abu Dhabi, Sharjah and Fujairah have their own employment centres, neighbourhoods, universities, cultural institutions and tourism economies.

A national railway begins to connect those individual urban systems. Suddenly, living in one city while regularly travelling to another becomes easier to imagine without every journey depending on a private vehicle.

That could have consequences beyond transportation. It could influence where people choose to live, where companies recruit employees, where families spend weekends, which destinations tourists visit, and even how businesses think about their potential customer base.

A railway does not simply shorten a journey. Over time, it can change what people consider to be within reasonable reach.


What will Etihad Rail trains be like?

Etihad Rail's passenger fleet consists of 13 trains, each capable of carrying up to 400 passengers, with operating speeds of up to 200 km/h.

Stations are also being designed as more than functional boarding points. Etihad Rail says they will include cafes, restaurants, retail outlets and other passenger facilities, while dining options will also be available onboard.

The existing Abu Dhabi to Fujairah service currently offers Comfort and Premium classes, with introductory fares starting at AED 55 for Comfort Class and AED 120 for Premium Class, though Dubai specific fares should be treated separately once confirmed for the new routes.

Tickets are available through Etihad Rail's digital booking channels, including its website and mobile application.


Dubai isn't the end of the rollout

September is one stage of a much larger network.

The current rollout has Dubai and Al Dhaid opening on September 30. Etihad Rail then plans to open the Madinat Zayed and Liwa stations in the Al Dhafra region on November 30, brought forward a month early to coincide with the region's festival season. The remaining Al Dhafra stations, at Al Sila, Al Dhannah and Mirfa, follow on December 30.

Sharjah's University City station, the network's eleventh and final stop, is scheduled for March 30, 2027.

The network is therefore arriving progressively rather than appearing overnight, and Etihad Rail expects annual ridership to exceed 36.5 million passengers by 2030 once the full eleven station network connecting 11 cities and locations, from Al Sila to Fujairah, is complete.


A different kind of UAE commute

The immediate temptation is to judge Etihad Rail by a simple question, is it faster than driving?

But that may not be the most interesting measure.

Driving between cities requires attention for the entire journey. Rail gives that time back. A passenger can work, read, watch something, have a conversation, or simply look out of the window.

For business travellers in particular, that distinction matters. Ninety minutes behind a steering wheel and ninety minutes sitting on a train may occupy the same amount of time on a clock, but they are not the same ninety minutes.

And as more stations open, the railway could make journeys that currently feel inconvenient become ordinary.


Dubai's railway era begins September 30

Dubai has spent decades building infrastructure around movement. Highways connected emerging districts. Dubai Metro changed how people moved through the city. The Tram added another layer to the Marina corridor.

Etihad Rail represents the next scale of that idea. Not neighbourhood to neighbourhood. Not station to station within Dubai. Emirate to emirate.

The first passenger trains are already running elsewhere in the country. More than 70,000 tickets were sold within the early phase. Now the network is approaching the point when Dubai becomes part of it.

On September 30, 2026, the opening of Dubai's Etihad Rail station will be more than another transport launch. It will be the day Dubai becomes connected to the beginnings of a national passenger railway.

And in a country where the car has defined intercity movement for generations, that could eventually change far more than the commute.

After years of relative calm along its southern frontier, Saudi Arabia is once again facing missiles, drones and an escalating conflict in neighbouring Yemen. The latest fighting is no longer only about Yemen. It is unfolding inside a much larger regional war involving Iran, and it now threatens both of the world's most important oil chokepoints at the same time.

For several years, Saudi Arabia appeared to be moving away from the war in Yemen.

The conflict had never formally disappeared, but after a UN-brokered truce in 2022, direct attacks between Saudi Arabia and Yemen's Houthi movement declined significantly. Front lines inside Yemen largely froze, and diplomatic efforts increasingly focused on preventing another major escalation.

That period of relative calm is now under serious pressure. Over the past week, Houthi forces have launched missiles and drones towards targets across Saudi Arabia, while Saudi-backed forces have intensified military operations against Houthi positions in Yemen. Saudi authorities have issued security alerts across several parts of the kingdom, including Jeddah and, for the first time since 2017, Mecca.

On the evening of September 16, the Saudi-led coalition said its air defences had intercepted a Houthi drone south of Mecca before it entered restricted airspace over the holy city. A coalition spokesperson called the security of Mecca's holy sites a red line. A Houthi military source rejected the claim, saying there was no threat directed at Mecca or any other holy site.

The confrontation that Saudi Arabia spent years trying to contain is becoming active again, and this time it is happening inside a much bigger regional war that most of the outside world is already watching closely.


How did Saudi Arabia and the Houthis get here?

The roots of the conflict go back more than a decade.

The Houthis, formally known as Ansar Allah, took control of Yemen's capital Sanaa in 2014 as Yemen's political order collapsed. Saudi Arabia entered the war militarily in 2015 at the head of a coalition supporting Yemen's internationally recognised government.

Iran has provided support to the Houthis, while Tehran and the group reject characterisations that reduce the Houthis to simply being an Iranian proxy. The relationship nevertheless made Yemen one of the major arenas of regional competition between Saudi Arabia and Iran.

Years of fighting followed. Saudi cities and infrastructure were targeted by Houthi missiles and drones, while Saudi-led airstrikes hit targets throughout Yemen. The conflict also produced an enormous humanitarian crisis.

Then came 2022. A UN-mediated truce significantly reduced large-scale fighting, and although the formal agreement eventually expired, much of the de-escalation held, roughly four years of relative quiet along the Saudi-Yemen frontier.


This is unfolding inside a much larger war

To understand why this particular escalation matters so much, it helps to understand what else has been happening in the region this year.

Since late February 2026, the United States and Iran have been in an active war, one that has already lasted longer than either side initially expected. The Strait of Hormuz, the narrow waterway between Iran and Oman through which roughly a fifth of the world's oil normally passes, has been largely closed since the war began, after Iran's Revolutionary Guard announced it was shutting the strait to vessels travelling to or from the United States, Israel and their allies.

A ceasefire in April briefly paused the fighting, and a memorandum of understanding signed in June outlined a path to end the war and reopen Hormuz over roughly sixty days. That agreement collapsed on July 8, when Iran began targeting commercial vessels in the strait to assert its claim over it. Fighting has continued since, including a large Iranian missile and drone barrage in early September that struck targets in Jordan, Bahrain, Kuwait and Iraq following renewed US strikes on Iran.

That is the backdrop the Houthi escalation against Saudi Arabia is now unfolding within. It is not a separate, unrelated conflict. It is a second front opening while the region's other major oil chokepoint is already effectively closed.


The conflict returned in July

The current Saudi-Houthi escalation did not begin this week.

In July, the Houthis launched missiles towards southern Saudi Arabia, including an attack aimed at Abha airport, after accusing Saudi Arabia of striking Sanaa airport. Reuters described those attacks as breaking roughly four years of relative calm between the two sides.

The situation deteriorated further as the broader regional confrontation involving Iran expanded through August. By September, the conflict had moved into a much more dangerous phase, with Houthi forces launching attacks against Saudi territory and energy infrastructure while advancing rapidly inside Yemen, and Saudi-backed Yemeni forces responding on the ground.

Saudi Arabia had again become directly exposed to a war it had spent years attempting to de-escalate, only this time alongside an active war between the United States and Iran that was already reshaping the region's oil map.


Why the Houthi advance inside Yemen matters

The most consequential developments may actually be happening inside Yemen itself.

On September 10 and 11, Houthi forces seized the strategic port city of Mocha on Yemen's Red Sea coast, then rapidly pushed south to take the rest of the coastline along with Perim Island, which sits in the middle of the Bab al-Mandeb Strait, and the Hanish Islands further north. The advance effectively gave the Houthis control of Yemen's entire Red Sea coastline and the waters around the strait within a matter of days.

That geography changes everything. Bab al-Mandeb is the narrow waterway separating Yemen from Djibouti and Eritrea, and ships travelling between the Indian Ocean and the Suez Canal normally pass through it. It is one of the world's critical maritime chokepoints for oil, container traffic and other goods moving between Asia, the Middle East and Europe.

With the Strait of Hormuz already largely closed by the US-Iran war, Bab al-Mandeb had become one of the Gulf's remaining reliable outlets. Houthi control over the strait's approaches now puts that route under pressure too, which is why analysts have described the Houthi advance as leaving Gulf states with an uncomfortable choice.


Saudi Arabia's oil infrastructure is part of the conflict

Saudi Arabia sits at the centre of the global energy system, which makes its oil infrastructure both strategically important and vulnerable during a regional conflict.

One particularly important piece of infrastructure is the kingdom's East-West pipeline, a 1,200-kilometre route built decades ago specifically so Saudi oil could move overland to the Red Sea if the Strait of Hormuz was ever closed. With Hormuz shut for most of this year, the pipeline had been carrying an estimated four to five million barrels a day, four to five percent of global oil supply, making it the kingdom's main escape valve.

On September 10 and 11, drone strikes launched from Iraqi territory hit the pipeline, causing fires at pumping stations and forcing Saudi Arabia to shut it down as a precaution. Iraq's government confirmed the drones had been launched from Maysan governorate in southern Iraq, where Iran-aligned militias operate, and dismissed a military commander over the incident, though no group has formally claimed the attack. Regional officials have told the Associated Press that Houthi forces helped plan and execute the strike alongside the Iraqi militias.

That leaves Saudi Arabia in a genuinely difficult position. Hormuz has been largely closed for months because of the US-Iran war. The kingdom's overland alternative has now been knocked offline by a drone strike. And the Houthis are simultaneously tightening their grip on the Red Sea route the pipeline was built to reach. Three routes, one crisis.

Oil markets have responded accordingly. Some physical crude cargoes in Europe were trading above $130 a barrel by September 15, nearing the record levels seen earlier in the year, as buyers sought alternatives to Middle Eastern supply affected by the overlapping disruptions.


Why are the Houthis attacking Saudi Arabia again?

The Houthis describe their attacks as retaliation for military action against them and for Saudi support of Yemen's internationally recognised government. Saudi Arabia, meanwhile, accuses the Iran-aligned movement of attacking civilian areas, military installations and strategic infrastructure.

The latest escalation has become intertwined with the wider regional conflict involving Iran, which makes the situation considerably more complicated than the earlier Saudi-Houthi confrontation. Saudi Arabia is no longer dealing only with an insurgent movement across its southern border. It is dealing with an armed group that now controls significant territory in Yemen, possesses missiles and drones, holds positions around one of the world's most important shipping lanes, and is operating within a broader regional war that is already reshaping how oil moves around the Gulf.


Saudi Arabia's difficult choice, and Washington's reluctance

Riyadh is balancing two objectives that increasingly conflict with one another. It wants to protect Saudi territory, energy infrastructure and shipping routes, but it also has strong reasons to avoid returning to the kind of prolonged military involvement in Yemen that characterised much of the previous decade.

Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman has reportedly called President Trump more than once in recent days, urging direct US strikes on Houthi positions as they closed in on Bab al-Mandeb. According to multiple reports, Trump has so far declined to commit US forces to direct strikes, instead offering intelligence sharing and targeting support, with roughly 200 US military personnel already in the kingdom providing non-combat assistance.

That leaves Saudi Arabia largely on its own in responding to the immediate threat, even as the war shaping the wider region continues without a clear resolution in sight.


What does this mean for the UAE?

For the UAE, developments in Saudi Arabia and Yemen are geographically close and economically relevant.

The immediate significance is not a direct military threat to Dubai or Abu Dhabi. It is the broader regional environment. Both the Strait of Hormuz and Bab al-Mandeb are crucial to Gulf trade, and disruption to either, let alone both at once, can affect oil prices, shipping costs, insurance premiums, airline routing and supply chains across the region.

The UAE also has a long history of involvement in Yemen and maintains significant political and economic interests around the Red Sea. So although the fighting is centred elsewhere, its economic consequences can spread quickly across the Gulf.


Is Saudi Arabia officially at war?

This is where terminology matters.

It would be misleading to describe the situation simply as a new conventional Saudi war, or to treat it as separate from what is already happening between the United States and Iran. Saudi Arabia and the Houthis never reached a comprehensive peace agreement ending their previous confrontation, what existed was a prolonged period of de-escalation, and that de-escalation is now breaking down inside a much larger regional conflict that has already been running for months.

Saudi-backed forces and the Houthis are fighting inside Yemen, Houthi missiles and drones are again being launched towards Saudi territory, and Saudi Arabia is taking military and defensive measures in response, all while the Strait of Hormuz remains largely closed because of the separate war between the United States and Iran.

The more accurate description is that the Saudi-Houthi conflict has sharply re-escalated as one part of a much wider Middle Eastern war.


What happens next?

The next few weeks will matter.

If attacks on Saudi territory continue, Riyadh may increase military pressure on Houthi-controlled areas, with or without direct US support. If the Houthis consolidate their position around Yemen's Red Sea coastline, maritime security around Bab al-Mandeb will become an even larger international concern. And if disruption around both Bab al-Mandeb and Hormuz continues simultaneously while repairs to the East-West pipeline are still weeks away, the consequences will increasingly be felt far beyond the Gulf.

Oil markets are already responding. Shipping routes are already under pressure. And after several years in which diplomacy appeared to be gradually pushing Saudi Arabia away from the Yemen war, the kingdom once again finds itself confronting the same fundamental problem on its southern border, only this time inside a war that is much larger than Yemen alone.

Apple's iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max officially go on sale across the UAE today, September 18. In Dubai, launch morning has already brought familiar queues, early arrivals and strong demand for Apple's latest flagship.

The wait is over.

Apple's iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max are officially available in the UAE from Friday, September 18, 2026, following pre-orders that opened on September 12. Apple confirmed the UAE as one of the first-wave markets for the new phones.

And in Dubai, launch day started early. Customers formed queues outside the Apple Store at Dubai Mall on Friday morning, with some shoppers reportedly arriving at around 3am to secure their preferred model, storage capacity and colour, continuing a pattern that has followed nearly every major iPhone launch in the city.

For UAE buyers who skipped the pre-order rush, the iPhone 18 Pro launch has now shifted from waiting for a delivery date to finding the configuration they actually want.


How much is the iPhone 18 Pro in the UAE?

Apple has priced the iPhone 18 Pro from AED 5,099, while the larger iPhone 18 Pro Max starts at AED 5,499.

Both models are available with 256GB, 512GB, 1TB and 2TB storage options, and buyers can choose between four finishes, Burgundy, Glacier, Silver and Black.

The new Burgundy finish appears to be attracting particular attention during the UAE launch, alongside the higher-capacity Pro Max configurations.

Apple is also offering trade-in credit for eligible older iPhones. According to its UAE launch information, customers trading in an iPhone 13 or newer can receive between AED 640 and AED 3,260 in instant credit, depending on the device and its condition, a discount worth checking before paying full price.


What's actually new?

The headline upgrade this year is not simply a faster processor. Apple has redesigned several of the technologies that define the Pro models.

At the centre is the new A20 Pro chip, featuring a six-core CPU, seven-core GPU with Neural Accelerators and a dual 16-core Neural Engine. Apple has also introduced a next-generation vapour chamber designed to improve sustained performance under demanding workloads.

The camera system receives one of the most significant upgrades. The iPhone 18 Pro introduces a 48MP Fusion Main camera with variable aperture, alongside 48MP Ultra Wide and 48MP Telephoto cameras. Variable aperture gives photographers more direct control over how much light enters the main camera, moving the iPhone another step toward the kind of creative control traditionally associated with dedicated cameras.

For people who mainly point, shoot and let computational photography handle everything else, that may not immediately change how they use an iPhone. For photographers and creators, however, it is one of the more interesting changes Apple has made to the iPhone camera in years.


The Dynamic Island is smaller

Apple has also reduced the size of the Dynamic Island. It remains part of the interface rather than disappearing entirely, but the smaller implementation gives more of the display back to content while retaining notifications and live activities.

Both Pro models continue to use Super Retina XDR displays with ProMotion and Always-On technology. The exterior is available in the four new colour combinations, while Apple has moved to an aluminium unibody construction for the Pro generation.


Battery life gets a substantial upgrade

Battery life is another major focus. Apple says the iPhone 18 Pro Max delivers the largest battery-life increase it has introduced on an iPhone. The Pro Max is rated for up to 45 hours of video playback, although actual battery performance will naturally depend on usage, connectivity, display brightness and other conditions.

Combined with the A20 Pro chip and improved thermal management, this may ultimately prove more useful to many buyers than some of the more visually obvious changes.


AI moves deeper into the iPhone

The iPhone 18 Pro ships with iOS 27, bringing Apple's latest Apple Intelligence features and Siri AI to the device.

That matters because the smartphone industry is gradually moving beyond AI being a collection of isolated features. Apple's direction is increasingly toward an iPhone that understands more context and can assist across different parts of the operating system. The A20 Pro's Neural Engine and GPU Neural Accelerators are designed partly around those increasingly demanding on-device AI workloads.

For Apple, the iPhone 18 generation therefore represents more than another annual hardware upgrade. It is also hardware designed for the company's next stage of AI integration.


Can you buy an iPhone 18 Pro in Dubai without a pre-order?

Yes, the phones officially entered retail availability on September 18.

But availability does not mean every configuration will remain in stock everywhere. Demand during the pre-order period was strong, with some configurations reportedly selling out within the first 20 minutes of pre-orders opening on September 12, and launch-day queues have continued that pattern.

Buyers looking specifically for combinations such as a Burgundy Pro Max or particular storage capacity may therefore find availability changing throughout launch week.

The safest approach is to check live availability before travelling to a store rather than assuming a specific configuration will be available for walk-in purchase.


Why Dubai remains an important iPhone launch market

Dubai's relationship with major smartphone launches is unusual.

New iPhone releases routinely attract buyers not only from the UAE but also from neighbouring countries and South Asia. This year is no different. UAE pricing puts the iPhone 18 Pro at roughly AED 30,000 less than India's official pricing once converted, before trade-in credit is even factored in, which is why some Indian buyers travel to Dubai specifically for the new Pro models.

That combination of relatively competitive pricing, international connectivity, large Apple retail locations and Dubai's enormous transient population makes the city an important regional destination whenever a major iPhone generation launches. It also explains why queues outside Dubai Mall have become almost an annual September ritual.


What about the iPhone Duo?

There is another major Apple launch still coming.

Apple's first foldable iPhone, the iPhone Duo, is not arriving alongside the iPhone 18 Pro today. Apple says UAE pre-orders for the Duo will begin on October 16, with the device starting at AED 8,499.

That creates an unusual decision for premium iPhone buyers this year. The iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max represent the familiar flagship iPhone refined with better cameras, performance, battery life and AI capabilities. The Duo represents something entirely different.

For anyone interested in Apple's first major change to the physical format of the iPhone, waiting another month may therefore be worth considering. For everyone else, Apple's newest Pro iPhones have officially arrived.

And judging by the queues forming in Dubai this morning, plenty of people were not interested in waiting.

Dubai's outdoor season is almost here. From Global Village and Dubai Safari Park to Miracle Garden, some of the city's most popular attractions are preparing to reopen after their annual summer break. Here are the dates confirmed so far for the 2026-27 season.

September in Dubai feels like a transition.

The temperatures are still high, but evenings gradually become more manageable. Outdoor terraces begin preparing for busier months, seasonal venues start announcing their return, and the city begins moving towards the period when much more of life happens outside.

For several of Dubai's biggest attractions, summer means closing completely. Global Village, Dubai Miracle Garden and Dubai Safari Park are among the destinations that pause operations during the hottest months of the year. The closures also give operators time to renovate, introduce new attractions and prepare for another winter season.

Now, the reopening calendar is beginning to take shape.


Dubai Safari Park, October 12

One of the first major attractions confirmed to return is Dubai Safari Park, which will reopen for Season 8 on October 12, 2026.

The wildlife park closed its previous season on June 22 after recording 144 animal births and expanding its international conservation affiliations.

For the new season, Dubai Safari Park is introducing the concept "Live More Wild Life", alongside a new Royal Safari Experience designed around smaller groups and private guided tours of up to ten guests over four hours.

The park is home to more than 3,000 animals across multiple zones, making its reopening one of the major dates on Dubai's autumn calendar.

Reopening: October 12, 2026


Global Village, October 14

Just two days later, another Dubai institution returns.

Global Village will officially open Season 31 on Wednesday, October 14, 2026, under the theme "A More Wonderful World". The new season will continue until May 2027.

Global Village has not yet revealed every new attraction coming this year, but it has confirmed that the upcoming season will introduce new and enhanced experiences alongside returning favourites. Entry pricing has been confirmed at AED 25 on weekdays and AED 30 on weekends, with free entry for children under three, guests aged 65 and over, and people of determination.

For many Dubai residents, the reopening of Global Village has effectively become an unofficial signal that winter is approaching. The destination combines country pavilions, street food, restaurants, shopping, live performances, carnival rides and entertainment across an enormous outdoor site.

Season 31 will operate from 4pm to midnight Monday through Thursday, extending until 1am Friday through Sunday. Tuesdays are reserved for families and ladies except when they fall on public holidays.

Reopening: October 14, 2026


Dubai Miracle Garden, October expected

The flowers are coming back too, although there is currently an important distinction.

Dubai Miracle Garden has not yet announced a specific opening day for its new season. The attraction's official website currently states that it is closed for summer renovation and will reopen for its October to May season.

The garden closed on May 31 following Season 14. During the summer closure, preparations take place for the millions of flowers and large-scale displays that make up the next season.

So for now, expected reopening is October 2026, with the exact date still to be announced. It is worth waiting for the official announcement rather than relying on older opening dates circulating online.


Dubai Garden Glow, autumn expected

Dubai Garden Glow is another attraction that traditionally disappears during the hottest part of the year.

The outdoor illuminated attraction closed for summer and has been expected to return during autumn, although an exact reopening date for the upcoming season has not yet been confirmed.

Its return normally coincides with cooler evenings, when outdoor attractions become considerably more comfortable.

Expected reopening: autumn 2026, exact date to be announced.


Ripe Market, autumn expected

Dubai's outdoor season is not only about major tourist attractions.

Ripe Market also pauses its main outdoor operations during summer before returning as temperatures fall. Its seasonal markets have become a familiar part of Dubai's cooler months, combining independent businesses, food, activities and community events.

The outdoor market is expected to resume during autumn, although its upcoming seasonal schedule should be confirmed closer to reopening.

Expected return: autumn 2026.


The dates to remember

For now, the Dubai outdoor calendar looks like this.

Attraction 2026 reopening
Dubai Safari Park October 12
Global Village October 14
Dubai Miracle Garden October, date TBA
Dubai Garden Glow Autumn, date TBA
Ripe Market Autumn, date TBA

The important dates are October 12 and 14. Those are confirmed. Miracle Garden and the other seasonal destinations should be treated as expected openings until their operators announce specific dates.


October is when Dubai changes

There is a reason so many openings cluster around the same few weeks.

Dubai's summer changes how the city functions. From roughly June through September, life shifts heavily indoors. Malls, restaurants, indoor entertainment and air-conditioned spaces become much more important while many outdoor destinations either reduce operations or close completely.

Then the balance begins shifting again. October brings back outdoor markets, parks, gardens, terraces, desert activities and major seasonal attractions. By November, the difference can feel dramatic. Places that were almost unusable during summer evenings become some of the busiest parts of the city.

Global Village's reopening is perhaps the clearest example. For residents who have lived in Dubai for years, its return has become less like the opening of another attraction and more like a seasonal marker.

Summer is ending. Dubai is going outside again.

Sheikh Ahmed bin Rashid Al Maktoum, the younger brother of Dubai's Ruler, Sheikh Mohammed bin Rashid Al Maktoum, passed away on Monday, September 21, 2026. Dubai has announced ten days of official mourning, with flags to fly at half-mast across the emirate.

Dubai is mourning the death of Sheikh Ahmed bin Rashid Al Maktoum, who passed away on Monday morning at the age of 76.

The Court of His Highness Sheikh Mohammed bin Rashid Al Maktoum announced the news, declaring a ten-day period of official mourning beginning September 21. UAE flags will be flown at half-mast across Dubai during the mourning period.

Sheikh Ahmed was the fourth and youngest son of the late Sheikh Rashid bin Saeed Al Maktoum, the former Ruler of Dubai, and a younger brother of Sheikh Mohammed bin Rashid Al Maktoum, Vice President and Prime Minister of the UAE and Ruler of Dubai.

Sheikh Mohammed pays tribute to his brother

Sheikh Mohammed shared a personal message mourning his brother, remembering him as someone who would remain in the family's hearts and prayers.

In his tribute, he wrote, "You are absent from our eyes but not from our prayers and hearts, O Ahmed." He also prayed for mercy for his brother and for patience and solace for his family and loved ones.

UAE President Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan extended his condolences to Sheikh Mohammed and the Al Maktoum family, saying Sheikh Ahmed's long-standing contributions to the development of the UAE since its founding continue to inspire the nation's journey of progress, and that his achievements "will remain vivid in memory."

Sheikh Hamdan bin Mohammed bin Rashid Al Maktoum, Crown Prince of Dubai and Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Defence, also mourned his uncle, sharing a prayer asking for mercy and forgiveness on his behalf.

Who was Sheikh Ahmed bin Rashid Al Maktoum?

Born on July 12, 1950, Sheikh Ahmed was a member of Dubai's ruling family whose career extended across public service, business and sport.

He graduated from the Royal Military Academy Sandhurst before joining Dubai's Central Military Command, where he later became Commander-in-Chief, developing the base into one of the leading military installations in the UAE. He subsequently served as Deputy Chairman of Dubai Police and Public Security.

Beyond his government responsibilities, Sheikh Ahmed was associated with major business and investment interests, including as Group Chairman of A.R.M. Holding and Dubai Real Estate Centre.

He also maintained a longstanding connection with Dubai's sporting community. Sheikh Ahmed served as president of Al Wasl Sports Club for more than six decades, and in the early 1990s he established the Jebel Ali Racecourse to promote horse racing in the UAE. He was also involved in founding the Dubai International Marine Club, serving as its first chairman when it launched in 1988.

Dubai announces official mourning

The ten-day mourning period began on Monday, September 21, 2026. The Ruler's Court confirmed that flags across Dubai will remain at half-mast during the official mourning period.

Sheikh Ahmed's passing marks the loss of a member of the generation closely associated with Dubai's development following the establishment of the United Arab Emirates. Condolences have been shared by the UAE's leadership and members of the Al Maktoum family.

Spain secured a dramatic 3-2 victory over England at Wembley Stadium on September 26, 2026.

Spain began their 2026/27 UEFA Nations League campaign with a dramatic 3-2 victory over England at Wembley Stadium on Saturday, September 26, overturning a 2-1 deficit in a match filled with early goals, defensive mistakes and a missed penalty.

Lamine Yamal opened the scoring inside two minutes before Anthony Gordon and Harry Kane turned the match around for England before half-time. However, the reigning world champions responded through second-half goals from Álex Baena and Mikel Oyarzabal, securing all three points in their opening Group A3 fixture.

UEFA Nations League, Group A3. Full time, September 26, 2026. England 2, Spain 3. Venue: Wembley Stadium, London.

Lamine Yamal strikes inside two minutes

Spain could hardly have asked for a better start.

Less than two minutes after kick-off, Lamine Yamal capitalised on a mistake from England defender Marc Guéhi, winning possession before curling the ball into the net. The early goal immediately put Thomas Tuchel's side under pressure and gave Spain the opportunity to control the opening stages. Ferran Torres briefly appeared to have doubled the visitors' advantage, but his effort was ruled out for offside.

England eventually found a response in the 36th minute. Jude Bellingham carried the ball forward before releasing Anthony Gordon, who finished past goalkeeper Unai Simón to bring the hosts level.

Just four minutes later, England completed the turnaround. Nico O'Reilly delivered a cross into the penalty area, and Harry Kane's header found the net following a deflection off Spain defender Marc Cucurella. England entered the break leading 2-1 despite Spain having enjoyed more possession and created several opportunities during the first half.


Harry Kane's missed penalty changes the momentum

The defining moment of the second half arrived when England were awarded a penalty following a challenge by Rodri on Jude Bellingham.

With England leading 2-1, Kane had the opportunity to extend the advantage and put Spain under further pressure. Instead, the England captain lost his balance and clipped the crossbar with his effort in the 54th minute. Notably, replays showed Kane's standing foot had touched the ball fractionally before his kicking foot made contact, meaning the goal would likely have been disallowed under IFAB rules even had it gone in.

Wembley had witnessed a potentially decisive moment. Spain responded almost immediately. Substitute Dani Olmo helped create an opportunity for Álex Baena, who curled his effort past England goalkeeper James Trafford to equalise in the 60th minute. The match was level again, and Spain had regained momentum.


Oyarzabal completes Spain's comeback

Spain's winning goal arrived in the 74th minute.

Baena, who had already scored the equaliser, turned provider with a pass that cut through England's defensive structure. Mikel Oyarzabal finished the move with a composed chip over Trafford, completing Spain's comeback and giving the visitors a 3-2 lead.

The goal was another significant contribution from a player who had previously scored the winner against England in the UEFA Euro 2024 final. England were unable to find another equaliser, leaving Spain to celebrate a victory in their first competitive match since winning the 2026 FIFA World Cup.


Spain's world champions begin another campaign with a statement

The match carried added significance because it brought together two teams that had reached the latter stages of the 2026 World Cup. Spain arrived at Wembley having defeated Argentina to become world champions, while England finished third after losing to Argentina in the semi-finals.

For Spain manager Luis de la Fuente, the result provided an encouraging start to another international campaign. His team demonstrated the ability to recover from a difficult first half and change the match through substitutions. Baena and Oyarzabal both made decisive contributions after entering the game, while Yamal's early goal established Spain's attacking threat from the opening minutes.

For England, the defeat highlighted several areas that will be examined ahead of their remaining Nations League fixtures. Tuchel's side showed attacking quality through Bellingham, Gordon and Kane, but defensive mistakes and the missed penalty contributed to a frustrating opening result.


What happens next for England and Spain?

Both teams will return to Nations League action on Tuesday, September 29. Spain will host Croatia at the Ramón Sánchez-Pizjuán Stadium in Seville, while England face Czechia away from home.

The two countries will meet again at the Riyadh Air Metropolitano in Madrid on November 15 in the final round of the league phase, a fixture that could prove decisive in Spain's bid to reach a fourth consecutive Nations League Finals. Overall, the two nations have now met 29 times, with England still holding the head-to-head edge on wins.

The opening match has already delivered one of the competition's early talking points. Spain's victory extends their recent run of significant results against England, following their 2-1 triumph in the Euro 2024 final. For England, attention now turns to recovering from the Wembley defeat and building momentum during the remaining group fixtures. For Spain, the comeback provides another chapter in a period that has seen the national team win the 2023 Nations League, Euro 2024 and the 2026 World Cup under De la Fuente.

RJ Mitte, the actor best known for playing Walter "Flynn" White Jr. in Breaking Bad, has died at the age of 34. Beyond one of television's most recognisable roles, Mitte became an important advocate for disability representation, drawing directly from his own experience living with cerebral palsy.

RJ Mitte, who played Walter White Jr. across all five seasons of AMC's Breaking Bad, died on Monday, October 12, in Brownsville, Texas. His representative confirmed his death to Variety, Deadline and People. He was 34.

A representative described Mitte as a beloved actor, philanthropist and disability-rights advocate, while asking for privacy for his family and loved ones. No cause of death was included in the representative's statement.

The news comes just days after Mitte had spoken publicly about Breaking Bad and reflected on what life might have looked like for Walter White Jr. after the end of the series. He had also been promoting a new film, Talking to Strangers, in recent interviews.


The actor behind Walter "Flynn" White Jr.

For millions of viewers, Mitte will always be associated with Walter White Jr., also known as Flynn, the teenage son of Walter and Skyler White in Breaking Bad.

Mitte appeared throughout the series from 2008 to 2013, sharing the screen with Bryan Cranston, Anna Gunn, Aaron Paul and the wider ensemble as the White family gradually collapsed under the consequences of Walter White's transformation.

Walter Jr. was not simply a background character. He became one of the clearest representations of what Walter White's decisions were doing to his family. For much of the show, Flynn idolised his father. By its final episodes, that relationship had completely broken apart.

One of Mitte's most memorable scenes came in the acclaimed episode "Ozymandias," when Walter Jr. finally learns the truth about his father and intervenes during a violent confrontation between Walter and Skyler. Mitte had discussed filming that sequence only days before his death, describing it as a defining moment for the character.


Cerebral palsy was part of the role, but never the whole character

Mitte lived with cerebral palsy, as did Walter Jr.

His condition was milder than his character's, but it gave Mitte an unusually personal connection to the role. AMC has noted that this experience allowed him to bring authenticity to the character while also becoming increasingly involved in organisations promoting equality and representation for people with disabilities.

That distinction was important. For years, disabled characters in film and television were frequently portrayed by actors who did not share their disability. Mitte's casting offered something different. His cerebral palsy was visible. It was acknowledged. But Walter Jr. was still allowed to exist as a teenager with anger, humour, loyalty, insecurity and complicated relationships.

The disability was part of him without becoming the entirety of the character. That helped make the role particularly significant for disability representation on mainstream television.


His work extended far beyond Breaking Bad

Although Breaking Bad remained Mitte's defining role, his career continued across television, film and advocacy work. His credits included appearances in projects such as Switched at Birth, Now Apocalypse and The Guardians of Justice, as well as film roles and independent productions.

But acting represented only one side of his public life.


RJ Mitte became a major advocate for disability representation

Mitte used the visibility he gained through Breaking Bad to advocate for people with disabilities in entertainment and beyond.

His representatives highlighted his work with United Cerebral Palsy and Shriners Children's, as well as his role as president of The Mitte Foundation. AMC's biography also documents his involvement with organisations including the National Disability Institute and campaigns advocating for performers with disabilities. In 2025, the Disability Rights Legal Center named him its Dream Award recipient.

For Mitte, representation was not just about seeing disabled people on screen. It was also about allowing them to be seen as complete people rather than stereotypes. The success of Breaking Bad gave him an enormous platform, and he continued using that platform long after the series ended.


Why Walter Jr. mattered so much to Breaking Bad

There is another reason Mitte's performance remains memorable. Walter Jr. represented something Breaking Bad needed, normality.

While Walter White descended deeper into violence, manipulation and criminal power, his son remained connected to ordinary life. Breakfast. School. Family arguments. Driving lessons. Teenage frustration. Those everyday moments made the extraordinary collapse of the White family feel more real.

Walter could justify his decisions to himself as being made "for his family." Walter Jr. increasingly became evidence of the opposite. His eventual rejection of his father is therefore one of the series' most emotionally important developments. The son Walter claimed to be protecting ultimately wanted nothing to do with him. Mitte gave that transformation credibility without turning the character into a simple moral device.


A role that became part of television history

Breaking Bad aired for five seasons between 2008 and 2013 and went on to become one of the most acclaimed television dramas of its era. The series won 16 Primetime Emmy Awards from 58 nominations and later expanded through Better Call Saul and the film El Camino.

Its cultural influence has continued more than a decade after the finale. Walter White, Jesse Pinkman, Saul Goodman and Gus Fring became some of modern television's most recognisable characters. Walter Jr. occupied a very different place in that world. He was never part of the criminal empire. That was precisely why he mattered.

His character gave audiences a view of the destruction from inside the White family rather than from inside Walter's criminal operation. And Mitte's performance ensured that Flynn remained more than simply "Walter White's son."


What is known about his death

Mitte died on Monday, October 12, in Brownsville, Texas. His representatives have not announced a cause of death, and a spokesperson for the local Justice of the Peace's office has said the matter is under investigation. Further details may emerge as authorities and his family provide additional information.


Remembering more than Flynn

It would be easy for the headline of Mitte's life to remain Breaking Bad. Few actors become associated with a television series watched and discussed on that scale.

But his legacy extends beyond Walter White Jr. Mitte helped normalise the presence of a disabled actor inside one of mainstream television's biggest productions. He then used the attention that role gave him to push for greater inclusion outside it.

That combination is why his death resonates beyond fans of a single series. He was part of a television phenomenon. He was also part of a broader effort to change who gets seen on screen and how they are represented.

At just 34, that work ends far earlier than anyone would have expected. But the character audiences knew as Flynn, and the advocacy Mitte built around his own experience, will remain part of the legacy he leaves behind.
