Dubai's economy reached AED473 billion in real GDP during the first six months of 2026, as strong growth in finance, healthcare, technology and construction helped offset pressure on trade, transport and real estate. The latest figures show a city still expanding in key future-facing sectors, even as regional disruption weighed on overall growth.

Dubai has released its latest economic figures, offering a clearer picture of how the city performed through one of the more challenging periods for regional trade and travel in recent years.

According to data from the Dubai Data and Statistics Establishment at Digital Dubai, real GDP reached approximately AED473 billion in the first half of 2026. That compares with AED484 billion during the same period in 2025, a 2.3% decline in real terms. GDP at current prices, however, edged up 0.2% to around AED505 billion.

The headline number therefore tells only part of the story. Several of Dubai's fastest-growing sectors continued to expand strongly, particularly financial services, healthcare, information and communications, and construction.


Finance is becoming an even bigger part of Dubai's economy

Financial and insurance activities were among the strongest-performing sectors during the first half of the year.

The sector expanded 8.8% in real terms, generating approximately AED65.9 billion in value added. Its share of Dubai's economy increased to roughly 14%, up from 12.5% during the same period a year earlier, making it the second-largest contributor to the economy after wholesale and retail trade.

That growth reflects the continued expansion of Dubai as an international financial centre. The Dubai International Financial Centre has continued attracting banks, asset managers, fintech companies, professional-services firms and family offices, and The National reports that the number of companies operating from DIFC exceeded 10,000 during the first half.

For Dubai, this is particularly important because finance is increasingly becoming one of the city's largest high-value sectors rather than simply a service supporting trade and real estate.


Healthcare was the fastest-growing major sector

Healthcare and social work recorded the strongest percentage growth among Dubai's major expanding sectors.

Economic activity in the sector increased 14.3% year on year, with its contribution rising from approximately AED5.4 billion to AED6.2 billion. That growth reflects the broader expansion of private healthcare, specialist clinics, medical tourism and health-related services across the emirate.

It is also another sign of Dubai's changing economic structure. The city's growth story is increasingly spread across sectors that did not historically dominate its economy.


Technology continued to expand

Information and communication activities grew 2.7%, reaching approximately AED24.7 billion during the first half.

That includes activity across telecommunications, digital services, software, cloud infrastructure and other technology-related industries. Dubai has spent several years positioning itself as a regional base for technology companies, particularly in areas such as artificial intelligence, fintech, digital commerce and enterprise software. Those sectors are becoming increasingly important as the city attempts to build more high-value, knowledge-based economic activity alongside its traditional strengths.


Construction remained positive

Construction grew 2.4% in real terms, contributing approximately AED33.2 billion to Dubai's economy during the period.

That expansion comes while Dubai continues to invest heavily in housing, aviation, transport and urban infrastructure. The National reports that approximately AED2.1 trillion in projects are moving forward across those areas, including the long-term expansion of Al Maktoum International Airport.

Those projects matter because construction spending often creates effects well beyond the sector itself. Airports create tourism capacity. Metro and road networks support new communities. Housing supports population growth. And large infrastructure projects can create new commercial districts around them.


But some of Dubai's biggest sectors contracted

The first-half figures also show clearly where the pressure came from.

Wholesale and retail trade, Dubai's single largest economic activity, declined 6% in real terms, although it still accounted for approximately 20.5% of GDP and rose 2% at current prices. Transport and storage fell 7.4%. Real estate activities contracted approximately 2.5% in real terms, although they grew 5.4% to AED65.1 billion when measured at current prices. Manufacturing slipped around 0.9%.

Those declines explain why overall real GDP fell despite significant growth elsewhere.


Regional disruption weighed heavily on travel and trade

One of the major reasons for the slowdown was regional instability during the first half of the year.

The National reports that the Iran war, which began on February 28, disrupted regional travel and trade, putting pressure on sectors including tourism, aviation, logistics and commerce. Dubai is unusually exposed to those sectors because it functions as a major global aviation, trade and logistics hub. When regional airspace, shipping routes or business travel are disrupted, the impact can appear quickly in economic data.

The UAE experienced a similar slowdown nationally. Real GDP across the country grew just 0.4% in the first half of 2026, reaching AED961.9 billion, while non-oil GDP expanded 1.8% and reached 79.2% of the total. Dubai's figures therefore sit within a wider regional economic context rather than representing an isolated local slowdown.


Dubai's economy is becoming more diversified

The most interesting part of the latest figures is not simply whether GDP moved up or down. It is which sectors are becoming more important.

For decades, Dubai's economy has been associated primarily with trade, aviation, tourism, real estate and construction. Those sectors remain enormous. But finance, healthcare, technology and professional services are taking a larger share of the economy.

Dubai H1 2026: key sectors

Sector H1 2026 real growth
Healthcare and social work +14.3%
Financial and insurance +8.8%
Electricity, water and waste +5.4%
Government services +2.9%
Information and communication +2.7%
Construction +2.4%
Education +1.2%
Manufacturing -0.9%
Real estate -2.5%
Wholesale and retail trade -6.0%
Transport and storage -7.4%

Figures are based on first-half data released by Digital Dubai and reported by Gulf News, WAM and The National.

The contrast is important. Some of Dubai's traditional economic engines weakened during the first half, while several sectors associated with the city's next phase of development continued growing. That is what economic diversification looks like in practice.


The first quarter had looked considerably stronger

Dubai's first-quarter figures had initially shown more momentum. Real GDP reached approximately AED232 billion in Q1 2026, representing annual growth of 2.4%.

The first-half figure therefore implies a much weaker second quarter. By simple arithmetic on the published figures, that points to a second-quarter decline of roughly 6% year on year, though Digital Dubai has not published that number directly. That broadly aligns with the national picture, where UAE real GDP fell 2.1% year on year in Q2 as regional disruption affected tourism, transport and trade.

This makes the timing of the slowdown particularly important. Rather than indicating uniform weakness throughout the year, the figures point toward a sharper disruption during the second quarter.


Dubai is still investing heavily into the next cycle

The city is continuing to pursue the Dubai Economic Agenda D33, which aims to expand Dubai's economy, strengthen its position as a global business centre and deepen activity across technology, trade, finance and advanced industries.

At the same time, the government continues to invest in infrastructure at a scale designed around long-term population and business growth. Al Maktoum International Airport is one of the largest examples. Transport networks are expanding. New residential districts continue to develop. Digital-commerce infrastructure is also growing, including a recently announced AED1.8 billion expansion of Dubai CommerCity, according to The National.

The strategy appears to be straightforward, continue building capacity even during periods of weaker short-term growth.


What the AED473 billion figure actually tells us

GDP headlines can sometimes oversimplify economic performance. Saying Dubai's economy reached AED473 billion sounds positive. Saying it declined 2.3% sounds negative. Both are true. The more useful interpretation lies between them.

Dubai experienced a noticeable slowdown during the first half of 2026, driven particularly by external disruption affecting trade, transport and other internationally exposed sectors. At the same time, finance, healthcare, technology and construction continued expanding. That suggests the city's economic base is broader than it was during previous regional disruptions. The sectors under pressure remain extremely important. But they are no longer carrying the economy alone.


A city increasingly built around several economies at once

Modern Dubai is difficult to describe through a single industry. It is simultaneously a tourism destination, financial centre, aviation hub, logistics platform, property market, technology base, healthcare destination and regional headquarters economy.

That complexity can create vulnerability when global events affect several sectors at once. But it can also provide resilience. When transport contracts, finance can grow. When trade weakens, healthcare or technology can continue expanding. That balance may ultimately be one of the most important developments in Dubai's economic transformation.

The AED473 billion first-half figure therefore represents more than an economic milestone. It shows an economy going through pressure while its internal structure continues to change. And increasingly, Dubai's growth story is no longer simply about how large the economy becomes. It is about what the economy is becoming.

Sheikh Mohammed bin Rashid Al Maktoum has opened nominations for the seventh edition of Arab Hope Makers, the region-wide initiative that recognises individuals and organisations creating meaningful social impact. The winner will receive AED1 million to help expand their work.

Dubai has opened the seventh edition of Arab Hope Makers, described as the largest initiative of its kind in the Arab world, dedicated to recognising people whose work improves the lives of others.

Sheikh Mohammed bin Rashid Al Maktoum, Vice President and Prime Minister of the UAE and Ruler of Dubai, announced the launch on Sunday, October 18, inviting people across the Arab world to nominate individuals, volunteer groups and non-profit organisations making a measurable difference in their communities, Khaleej Times reports.

The winner will receive AED1 million, with applications and nominations now open through the official platform, arabhopemakers.com.


What is Arab Hope Makers?

Sheikh Mohammed launched Arab Hope Makers in 2017 through a social media announcement offering AED1 million for the role of Hope Maker. The programme is run by the Mohammed bin Rashid Al Maktoum Global Initiatives (MBRGI) and highlights people and organisations that voluntarily work to improve lives without seeking profit.

Eligible work includes projects, campaigns, programmes and creative initiatives that alleviate suffering, address local challenges or help communities progress socially, economically, culturally and educationally. Efforts that improve access to education, healthcare and a dignified life are also among those the initiative seeks to recognise.

Applicants can nominate themselves or be nominated by someone else.


Sheikh Mohammed calls for 'role models'

Announcing the latest edition, Sheikh Mohammed described Hope Makers as role models who have made acts of kindness part of everyday life. He said:

"Nurturing hope is a triumph for life itself. The hope we cultivate today will yield prosperity, peace and safety in people's lives tomorrow."

He also encouraged people working to improve their communities to apply, and urged the public to nominate those whose contributions deserve recognition.

The initiative is built around the idea that social impact does not always come from large institutions. It can begin with an individual, a volunteer group or a local organisation solving one problem in one community. Arab Hope Makers attempts to identify those stories and give them a much larger platform.


More than 335,000 Hope Makers have participated

The scale of the initiative has grown significantly since its launch.

When the first edition was announced in 2017, organisers expected around 20,000 submissions. Instead, more than 65,000 were received from individuals, volunteer groups and humanitarian and community organisations across the Arab world.

The sixth edition attracted more than 15,800 participants, bringing the total number of Hope Makers across the first six editions to more than 335,000. For the seventh edition, organisers are aiming to collect tens of thousands of stories.


The last winner helped thousands of children receive surgery

At the most recent awards ceremony, Sheikh Hamdan bin Mohammed bin Rashid Al Maktoum, Crown Prince of Dubai, Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Defence, named Moroccan humanitarian Fouzia Jbara Mahmoudi the winner.

Mahmoudi received the AED1 million award for her work with Operation Smile, a foundation that helps children born with cleft lips and palates. Her initiative has facilitated more than 19,000 surgeries.

The other two finalists were also awarded AED1 million each on Sheikh Hamdan's direction, bringing the total prize money for the sixth edition to AED3 million. Kuwait's Hend Alhajri founded Fatima House in Tanzania, which provides a home for orphaned children. Morocco's Abderrahmane Rais launched a humanitarian initiative supporting widows and women in need.


The prize is intended to make the work bigger

The AED1 million award is not simply recognition. Arab Hope Makers also provides financial support to help selected Hope Makers expand their work and reach more people, promoting a culture of generosity, optimism and community service across the Arab world.

Mohammad Al Gergawi, Secretary-General of MBRGI, said the initiative draws on Sheikh Mohammed's vision of spreading optimism, countering despair and recognising people who serve their communities without expecting anything in return. He said it shines a light on the potential and talents dedicated to improving people's lives, by helping communities access education, healthcare and a dignified life.


Who can apply?

The seventh edition is open to individuals, volunteer groups and non-profit organisations across the Arab world. Eligible work can span areas including:

  • humanitarian assistance
  • healthcare
  • education
  • social and economic development
  • community support
  • cultural and creative initiatives that address local challenges

Applicants can nominate their own work, while members of the public can also nominate someone whose contribution they believe deserves recognition. Applications are open through arabhopemakers.com.


Why the initiative matters to Dubai

Although Arab Hope Makers reaches far beyond the UAE, Dubai is where the programme is coordinated and amplified. It fits a wider model the emirate has increasingly adopted: using its global visibility, institutions and media reach to support initiatives with regional impact.

For Dubai, that extends the city's identity beyond business, tourism and infrastructure. It positions the emirate as a platform where social projects from across the Arab world can gain visibility, funding and international attention.

The strongest stories in Arab Hope Makers are usually not about large organisations. They are about individuals who noticed a problem around them and decided to act. That remains the central idea of the seventh edition.

The AED1 million prize is significant, but the initiative is ultimately built around something simpler: finding people already creating hope, and giving them the means to create more of it.

The UAE has launched a nationwide artificial intelligence initiative that lets residents create websites and digital applications without writing traditional code. Announced on Thursday, 29 October 2026, UAE Vibe Codes was developed by the UAE Artificial Intelligence Office in collaboration with Microsoft, and it attracted 5,000 participants in its first hour, according to the Emirates News Agency (WAM).

It was introduced as part of UAE Codes Day 2026, which this year adopted vibe coding as its theme. In vibe coding, people describe what they want to build in everyday language and AI turns those instructions into a working prototype.

A nationwide launch with 5,000 sign-ups in an hour

The programme is aimed at a broad audience, including students, educators, entrepreneurs, business owners and employees in government and private organisations. Omar Sultan Al Olama, the UAE's Minister of State for Artificial Intelligence, said it is intended to help people benefit from rapid advances in digital development and build confidence in their ability to innovate.

He also said the value of AI lies in expanding human innovation and helping people turn ideas into reality.

The launch announcement did not give a total budget or say how many finished applications participants have produced. The 5,000 figure reflects early participation, not independently verified software projects.

What vibe coding is and how it works

Building a website or app has traditionally required programming languages, frameworks and technical infrastructure. With AI-assisted coding, a user can describe the result they want in natural language, such as an app to organise household expenses, manage customer enquiries or track appointments. An AI tool generates an initial version, and the user can keep giving instructions to change the design, add features or fix problems.

WAM lists workplace tools, daily task apps, startup projects and educational resources among the possible uses.

There is an important gap between a prototype and software that is ready for customers. Applications that handle payments, confidential information or sensitive business records still need security, testing and maintenance. Vibe coding speeds up experimentation, but it does not remove the need for technical oversight once a project becomes a real service.

How to join the free course

The experience is available online at uaecodesday.specnt.com. According to the programme's website, the course is free, takes about 10 minutes, needs no sign-up and is open to people aged 15 and above. Although WAM's announcement describes the invitation as open regardless of age, the site sets the 15-and-over limit.

The site outlines three steps:

  • Learn: six short units introducing vibe coding and how natural-language instructions can build applications.
  • Build: write a prompt describing an idea and use the platform's AI tools to generate a prototype.
  • Certificate: download a UAE Codes Day certificate after finishing.

The course is meant as a quick introduction, not a software engineering qualification. For residents, it offers a low-barrier way to try the idea. Students can experiment with learning tools, professionals can look at automating repetitive tasks, and entrepreneurs can test an early concept before committing to a larger build.

Partners and public outreach

Microsoft is the technology collaborator on the initiative. The UAE Artificial Intelligence Office is also running practical workshops with Google, Emirates Global Aluminium, Siemens and IBM, which take participants from identifying a challenge to building an initial digital solution.

UAE Codes Day activities involve a wide range of organisations, including Dubai's Roads and Transport Authority, the Ministry of Education, the Ministry of Justice, the UAE Space Agency, Emirates Health Services, Emirates NBD, Etisalat UAE, du and Furjan Dubai.

The AI Office is also working with Emaar and cinemas across the UAE to promote the initiative on digital screens. Taking the message to places where residents already spend time, rather than only to universities and conferences, is a notable part of the approach.

What it could mean for Dubai's businesses

For businesses, the most relevant effect is a shorter route to testing a digital idea. Small companies often spot ways to improve operations but lack the budget to commission custom software straight away. AI-assisted building could make those first steps more accessible.

A restaurant operator might try an internal stock-tracking screen, a property consultant might prototype a way to organise client enquiries, and a small retailer might sketch an order dashboard. These are illustrations, not projects confirmed to have come out of UAE Vibe Codes.

For startups, it could mean faster early experimentation. For established firms, it could help non-technical staff explain what they need more clearly to developers.

Professional developers and agencies may increasingly stand out through reliability, user experience, accessibility, integration and security. The initiative is better read as a way to widen participation in software creation than as a sign that professional expertise is no longer needed.

The AI Office responds to claims the website was fake

The launch also raised a trust issue. Khaleej Times reported that the UAE AI Office responded to social media posts claiming that a government website tied to UAE Vibe Codes was fraudulent. The posts followed SMS invitations encouraging residents to visit the site.

The AI Office said the website is authentic and belongs to an official government entity, and encouraged the public to verify information through official sources before sharing claims. Residents who completed the course shared their experiences online.

The episode shows the challenge facing digital public programmes: people need dependable ways to tell genuine government messages from suspicious ones. The address confirmed in WAM's launch announcement is uaecodesday.specnt.com.

Part of a wider UAE AI skills push

UAE Vibe Codes sits alongside other national efforts to build AI skills. On 7 October 2026, Abu Dhabi's Department of Government Enablement launched AiNative, a training programme developed with OpenAI, Microsoft and Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence. It aims to train 20,000 Abu Dhabi government employees in AI by the end of 2026, with public access planned for a later phase.

These programmes serve different audiences, so their targets should not be added together into one national figure.

UAE Codes Day itself has deep roots. In October 2021, Sheikh Mohammed bin Rashid Al Maktoum, Vice President and Prime Minister of the UAE and Ruler of Dubai, directed that 29 October be observed annually as UAE Codes Day. The date marks the launch of the region's first e-government initiative on 29 October 2001. In November 2023, UNESCO adopted the UAE's proposal to designate 29 October as the International Day of Programming.

The real test is what residents build next

Early interest in UAE Vibe Codes is strong, but participation numbers alone will not show its impact. The more useful measures will be how many people keep experimenting after the introductory course, whether businesses adopt useful prototypes, and whether participants develop the skills to improve and maintain what they build.

As of 30 October 2026, the announced results show strong early uptake but no evidence of long-term adoption or measurable economic benefit.

That matters in a city like Dubai, where digital services run through tourism, property, retail, hospitality and business operations. Easier software creation could encourage more people to solve everyday problems with technology, though turning experiments into dependable products will take more learning, investment and technical judgement.

The initiative is not proof that anyone can become a software engineer in 10 minutes. It is an attempt to make the first experience of building digital technology far simpler, and the open question for Dubai is whether that leads to useful ideas, better services and new businesses.

Cristiano Ronaldo has ended his international career. On Thursday 5 November 2026, the 41-year-old announced in a long video on Instagram that he is retiring from Portugal duty after 23 years, closing the most decorated chapter in the country's football history.

"The day has come to hand back the number seven shirt of the national team that belongs to us all," he said, adding that he never felt the shirt was exclusively his.

What Ronaldo said

The message was personal rather than procedural. He described a journey that began in August 2003 and spoke about the people he had met through the shirt, including emigrant Portuguese communities who felt closer to home for 90 minutes at a time. He acknowledged defeats that were still hard to recall and moments when he could not give supporters what they wanted, but said he never stopped feeling proud to represent Portugal.

He closed by looking forward, saying Portugal will always need young people who dream and new generations who believe they can reach places no one has reached before.

Why now: the row with Jorge Jesus

The announcement did not come out of nowhere. It follows a fall-out with Portugal coach Jorge Jesus, his former Al Nassr manager, over playing time.

According to ESPN, Ronaldo was an unused substitute in Portugal's 2-1 win at Norway, the first time that had happened in 18 years for his country. He then walked out of the squad during the same international window. The Portuguese federation responded in October with a 30-day suspension and a €255 fine.

Ronaldo apologised to his teammates and said he wanted to keep playing for Portugal. He did not apologise to Jesus, whom he accused of breaking promises about his role. The suspension had only just ended when he made his announcement, one day before Jesus was due to name his squad for the Nations League games against Denmark and Wales.

His international career in numbers

Record Detail
Caps 234 (men's international record)
Goals 146 (men's international record)
Debut August 2003
Major trophies Euro 2016, UEFA Nations League 2019 and 2025
World Cups played Six, the latest this summer
Missing from the CV The World Cup

How Portugal responded

The Portuguese Football Federation issued a statement thanking him for an "absolutely extraordinary" career and describing him as an inspiring leader and the ultimate symbol of the national team's spirit. It said it intends to organise a tribute worthy of his career, with details to come, and ended with a nod to his next target: "Let's go for goal number 1,000!!!"

Former clubs including Manchester United, Sporting CP and Juventus also paid tribute.

The club career goes on

Retiring from Portugal does not mean Ronaldo is hanging up his boots. He will continue at Al Nassr in Saudi Arabia and is expected to finish his club career at the end of this season, according to ESPN. He currently sits on 985 career goals and is still pursuing 1,000.

That chase matters beyond the statistics. With international games gone, every remaining goal will have to come in club football, which makes the rest of this season a countdown of sorts.

A Gulf connection

Ronaldo's move to the Saudi Pro League also brought him regularly into the Gulf's sporting calendar. In December 2025, he collected the Best Middle East Player award at the Globe Soccer Awards, held at Atlantis The Royal in Dubai, his third win in that category in as many years since it was introduced. For fans in the UAE, the retirement is a farewell to the national-team Ronaldo, not to the one they can still watch in the region.

A generation's farewell

ESPN notes that Ronaldo retires less than a month after his long-time rival Lionel Messi played his last game for Argentina. The two players defined an era of football, and within weeks both have left the international stage.

Ronaldo's own words suggest how he would like it remembered. Goals come and go, he said, trophies end up in museums and records are eventually broken, but the place we hold in people's hearts is something time cannot erase.

Sources: ESPN (5 November 2026), Gulf News and Khaleej Times reporting on the Globe Soccer Awards, Portuguese Football Federation statement as quoted by ESPN.

The Emirates Group has reported a 66% fall in half-year profit as the regional conflict, soaring fuel costs and disrupted air travel weighed on Dubai's largest aviation business. Announced on 5 November 2026, the results show a profit before tax of AED4.1 billion (US$1.1 billion) for the six months to 30 September, against AED12.2 billion in the same period last year, which was a record. Revenue fell 12% to AED66.2 billion.

The Group, which includes Emirates airline and the aviation services provider dnata, stayed profitable through what its chairman called a demanding six months.

The Group's numbers at a glance

Indicator First half of 2026-27 Change
Profit before tax AED4.1 billion Down 66%
Profit after tax AED3.6 billion Down 66%
Revenue AED66.2 billion Down 12%
EBITDA AED12.5 billion Down 41%
Cash balance AED54.1 billion Down from AED59.6 billion at 31 March 2026

The Group said it drew on its cash reserves to cover aircraft pre-delivery payments and debt servicing, and it paid the remaining AED2 billion of the AED3.5 billion dividend declared for 2025-26 to its owner, the Investment Corporation of Dubai. Headcount stood at 128,237 on 30 September, 2% lower than at the end of March.

Sheikh Ahmed bin Saeed Al Maktoum, Chairman and Chief Executive of Emirates airline and Group, said customer demand held firm and cargo made a strong contribution, even as global jet fuel prices doubled. He thanked the UAE government for coordinating the safe resumption of air transport after military activity across the Gulf region, and said the Group enters the second half with measured optimism.

Emirates airline: a smaller operation, a much smaller profit

Emirates airline reported a profit before tax of AED3.7 billion, down 68% from AED11.4 billion a year earlier. Its profit after tax was AED3.3 billion, down 66%, and revenue fell 13% to AED56.9 billion.

The company said intermittent airspace restrictions and closures across the region, along with government travel advisories, reshaped travel flows. Bloomberg and other outlets link the disruption to the Iran war. By 30 September, Emirates was operating 91% of its pre-disruption network, serving 150 airports in 78 countries and territories.

Traffic was sharply lower:

  • Passengers: 21.8 million carried between 1 April and 30 September, down 22%.
  • Capacity: available seat kilometres fell 17%, and overall capacity in tonne kilometres fell 10%.
  • Seat factor: 72.0%, down from 79.5%.

To rebuild confidence, the airline introduced an industry-first travel cover that is not restricted by government travel advisories, free date changes and generous refund policies. Premium cabins continued to see strong demand.

Fuel: the biggest cost hit, cushioned by hedging

Global jet fuel prices roughly doubled compared with the same period last year. Emirates burned 12% less fuel as flying was cut, yet its fuel bill before hedging rose 60%. Gains of AED7.1 billion from its fuel price risk management programme brought the net increase down to 13%. Fuel remains the largest cost for the airline, at 34% of operating costs.

Total operating costs fell only 2%, broadly in line with the reduction in operations.

Cargo: the bright spot

Emirates SkyCargo carried 1.2 million tonnes, down just 1%, but cargo revenue jumped 52%. The Group said the regional conflict reduced available airfreight capacity while disruption to marine transport pushed shippers towards air.

The division took delivery of five new Boeing 777 freighters and its first passenger-to-freighter converted aircraft. It added freighter services to Almaty and Zhengzhou and launched dedicated freighter flights to more than 15 existing destinations.

dnata: profit halves

dnata reported a profit before tax of AED410 million, down 51%, on revenue of AED11.0 billion, down 7%. The Group attributed the decline to reduced volumes in some of its UAE and UK businesses. Its international operations helped offset lower airline and travel traffic in the UAE and Gulf region.

dnata division Detail
Airport operations Revenue AED5.4 billion, down 3%; 414,012 aircraft turns handled, down 8%
Flight catering and retail Revenue AED4.2 billion, up 1%; 54.0 million meals, down 10%
Travel Revenue AED1.4 billion, down 31%, mainly due to the divestment of Travel Republic and Netflights

dnata kept investing, opening a new integrated cargo command centre in Dubai, commissioning an AED100 million logistics facility in Dubai South and committing AED8 million to expand The Fort - Lisaili, the desert tourism destination run by Arabian Adventures. It also secured a seven-year ground handling licence at Amsterdam Schiphol.

Investment continues despite the squeeze

Emirates did not pause its fleet and product programmes. In the half-year it received nine Airbus A350s and completed cabin refurbishments on 12 aircraft (nine A380s and three Boeing 777s) as part of a retrofit programme worth more than US$7 billion. It fitted Starlink Wi-Fi to 36 more aircraft, bringing the total to 57, and broke ground in May on a US$5.1 billion engineering and maintenance facility at Al Maktoum International Airport, due for completion in the mid-2030s.

New passenger products included an Economy headrest and electronically controlled privacy dividers in Premium Economy, and the airline opened new concept lounges in Munich, Frankfurt and Manchester. It also extended its sponsorships of Arsenal (to 2033) and Real Madrid (to 2031).

What it means for Dubai

Emirates is one of Dubai's largest employers and a key driver of its connectivity, so the results ripple through the wider economy. The Group's own figures show some of the knock-on effects: Emirates Flight Catering's external revenue fell 51% as airport traffic dropped, and Emirates Leisure Retail and MMI revenue fell 13% on lower tourism traffic in the UAE.

The results also show how exposed Dubai's hub model is to regional airspace and security conditions. Emirates connects passengers between Europe, Asia, Africa and the Americas through Dubai, so disruption in the Gulf hits the network directly. At the same time, Emirates' passenger numbers should not be read as a direct measure of Dubai's total tourism, which also depends on visitors arriving through other airlines and routes.

For investors and businesses, the key point is that the Group remained profitable, with AED54.1 billion in cash, despite a sharp drop in traffic and a doubling in fuel prices. The chairman said the government's measures had eased travel advisories to and through the UAE, which supported the restoration of operations.

The second half

Emirates enters the second half of its financial year facing continued uncertainty over fuel prices, regional security and travel demand. Its recovery will depend partly on the stability of regional airspace, passenger confidence and global fuel costs, while strong cargo demand and heavy hedging gains have so far provided a cushion.

The first-half figures mark a steep fall from last year's record. They also show a business that kept investing in fleet, product and infrastructure while earning a profit in unusually difficult conditions. For Dubai, the recovery of its flagship airline remains closely tied to the city's position as a global aviation, tourism and business hub.

British comedian, actor and broadcaster Russell Brand has been found guilty of rape and sexual assault. A jury at Southwark Crown Court in London convicted the 51-year-old on Thursday 5 November 2026 of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault, following a trial that began in mid-October. He was taken into custody and will be sentenced on Monday 9 November. No sentence has yet been imposed.

The verdicts

Brand had pleaded not guilty to all charges. The jury convicted him on four counts and acquitted him on three, according to Reuters.

Charge Verdict
Rape (one woman, 2009) Guilty
Sexual assault (three women, between 2004 and 2009) Guilty on three counts
Two further charges of rape Not guilty
Attempted indecent assault Not guilty

The trial heard from six complainants, covering allegations between 1999 and 2009. None of the women knew each other, and all came forward after a television documentary and press reports in 2023. All are entitled to lifelong anonymity.

Judge Joel Bennathan told the court Brand would be sentenced on Monday and faces a lengthy prison term.

The prosecution and the defence

Prosecutors described Brand as a "ruthless" sexual predator who exploited women while his career grew from small stand-up venues to television and Hollywood. The convictions relate to incidents in London involving women he met through his work and social life.

Brand denied the allegations throughout. He maintained that his sexual encounters were consensual, or that the allegations were fabricated. The jury's acquittals on three charges show it did not accept every allegation brought by the prosecution.

Detective Superintendent Andy Furphy of the Metropolitan Police called the convictions a testament to the courage and determination of the women who came forward, and said Brand used his influence, status and fame to exploit and sexually offend against women.

How the case began

The police investigation followed a joint investigation by The Times, The Sunday Times and Channel 4's Dispatches, published in September 2023. Further women then contacted police, and the Crown Prosecution Service later authorised charges. Brand entered his pleas in 2025 and 2026, before the jury was selected in October.

From British comedian to Hollywood star

Brand rose to prominence in Britain in the early 2000s through stand-up, television presenting and radio, including work linked to Channel 4's Big Brother franchise. He moved into film with roles in Forgetting Sarah Marshall (2008), Get Him to the Greek (2010) and Arthur (2011), and married American singer Katy Perry in 2010. The marriage ended in divorce.

In later years he shifted from mainstream entertainment to online commentary, building a large international following through videos on politics, media, health and spirituality.

What happens next

Sentencing is scheduled for Monday 9 November at Southwark Crown Court. Convicted defendants in England and Wales can seek permission to appeal, but no decision on that has been reported.

The case has renewed debate about how powerful figures in the entertainment industry are held to account, and about the difficulty of prosecuting non-recent sexual offences. The women at the centre of it, whose identities are protected by law, spent weeks giving evidence about events that took place between 15 and 20 years ago. The next step is the court's decision on sentence.

Renewing a driving licence in the UAE has become a largely digital process. In Dubai, drivers aged 21 and over pay AED300 for renewal, plus an AED20 Knowledge and Innovation fee and the cost of an electronic eye test. Costs, eligibility and procedures vary by issuing emirate, by the driver's age and by whether the licence has already expired, so a little preparation can avoid delays and penalties.

How long is a renewed licence valid?

Validity depends on age, nationality and residency status, according to the RTA.

Driver category Renewal validity
UAE and GCC citizens aged 21 and over 10 years
Residents aged 21 and over 5 years
Drivers younger than 21 1 year

Drivers aged 21 and over can renew up to six months before expiry. Drivers younger than 21 can renew up to three months before.

How to renew a Dubai licence

Dubai-issued licences are renewed through the RTA, using its website and apps. The usual steps are:

  • Take an eye test. Visit an RTA-approved centre, which submits the result electronically.
  • Sign in. Use your Emirates ID or UAE Pass details on the RTA website or app.
  • Check your details. Confirm your personal information, licence and eye-test result.
  • Clear any fines. Outstanding traffic fines must be paid first.
  • Pay. Settle the renewal fees electronically.
  • Receive the licence. Access it digitally or choose physical card delivery.

A valid Emirates ID is required. The RTA says that someone holding only a visit visa cannot renew an expired Dubai licence.

Fees for 2026

The renewal fee depends on age, and every applicant pays the AED20 Knowledge and Innovation fee.

Dubai renewal expense Amount
Licence, aged 21 and over AED300
Licence, younger than 21 AED100
Knowledge and Innovation fee AED20
Electronic eye test AED140 to AED180
Standard card delivery AED20
Same-day delivery AED35
Delivery within two hours AED50
Delivery to GCC countries AED50

That puts a standard renewal at about AED460 to AED500 for drivers aged 21 and over, and AED260 to AED300 for those younger than 21, including the eye test and the Knowledge and Innovation fee. These figures exclude delivery and any outstanding fines.

Professional drivers need a medical fitness examination, which the RTA says is valid for 11 months. The RTA also offers a mobile truck service for the eye test, renewal and delivery, listed at AED1,000.

Eye tests: 434 approved centres

An eye test remains valid for three years, so drivers with a recent qualifying test on file may not need to repeat it. On 3 August 2026, the RTA announced that 100 new approved centres had been added in the first half of the year, a 30% increase that takes the total to 434. Centres completed 940,728 eye-test transactions in 2025 and 854,213 in the first six months of 2026.

If your licence has expired

Dubai charges a renewal delay fine of AED10 per month, calculated from the expiry date and capped at AED500. That fee is separate from the penalty for driving on an expired licence. Under the Dubai Police penalty table published on the Aman Roads platform, driving with an expired licence carries an AED500 fine, 4 black points and seven days of vehicle impoundment.

Item Amount or penalty
Renewal delay fine AED10 per month, capped at AED500
Driving with an expired licence AED500 fine, 4 black points, 7-day impound

If your licence expired more than 10 years ago, the process is different and costs more. You must book and pass an evaluation test, and the RTA fee list includes a training file (AED200), a learning application (AED100), a handbook (AED50) and the evaluation test itself (AED200), on top of the licence fee, the Knowledge and Innovation fee, the eye test and the delay fine.

Other emirates

The renewal platform depends on who issued the licence:

Emirate Main digital service
Dubai RTA
Abu Dhabi TAMM (Abu Dhabi Mobility)
Sharjah, Ajman, Umm Al Quwain, Ras Al Khaimah, Fujairah Ministry of Interior services (generally)

Fees and requirements differ, so check with the issuing authority before paying. If you hold a Dubai licence but your residence visa is from another emirate, the RTA addresses this case in its FAQs, so confirm the rules before applying.

Before you renew

Most problems come from three things: an expired Emirates ID, unpaid traffic fines, or a missing eye-test result. Check your traffic file, complete the eye test in advance and use the official platform for the emirate that issued your licence. Rules, fees and platforms can change, so confirm current details with the RTA, TAMM or the Ministry of Interior before you apply.

The shift to online renewal is part of a broader move to digital government services in the UAE. For most Dubai residents aged 21 and over, it means a single online transaction costing roughly AED460 to AED500, and several years of validity afterwards.

Nitesh Tiwari's Ramayana: Part One has opened with the biggest pre-Diwali Hindi debut on record. Released on Thursday 5 November 2026, three days before Diwali, the mythological epic starring Ranbir Kapoor, Sai Pallavi and Yash earned ₹64.85 crore net and ₹77.5 crore gross in India on its first day, according to trade tracker Sacnilk. Sacnilk's estimate for the worldwide gross is ₹127.5 crore.

For audiences in Dubai and across the UAE, where the film is now in cinemas, the release carries extra weight. Its story is told and debated across South Asia, and its villain, Ravana, the legendary King of Lanka, holds a very different place in Sri Lankan tradition.

The opening-day numbers

Sacnilk's figures, which it describes as final for India and provisional for overseas markets, are as follows.

Opening-day measure Sacnilk figure
India net ₹64.85 crore
India gross ₹77.5 crore
Overseas gross (estimate) about ₹50 crore
Worldwide gross (estimate) ₹127.5 crore

Hindi was the biggest contributor, earning ₹47.5 crore net across more than 20,000 shows, ahead of the Kannada version (₹7.25 crore), Telugu (₹6 crore), Tamil (₹2.6 crore) and Malayalam (₹1.5 crore). Sacnilk reported about $2 million from North American premieres and a further $1.5 million on Thursday, via Venky Box Office.

The Hindi opening beat Tiger 3 (₹43 crore), which opened on Diwali day in 2023, making it the highest first-day Hindi net for a film released before the festival. Sacnilk cautions that the comparison has limits, because Tiger 3 and other Diwali releases benefited from post-festival growth. It is also the third-biggest Bollywood opening of 2026, behind Dhurandhar 2: The Revenge (₹99.1 crore) and Drishyam 3: The Conclusion (₹62 crore).

It is not the largest opening in Indian cinema. Against Adipurush, the 2023 adaptation of the same epic, Ramayana won on Hindi net (₹47.5 crore vs ₹37.25 crore) but trailed on total India net (₹64.85 crore vs ₹86.75 crore), because Adipurush drew most of its opening from Telugu audiences.

The cast and the team

Ranbir Kapoor plays Rama and Sai Pallavi plays Sita. Yash, best known for the KGF films, plays Ravana. Sunny Deol plays Hanuman and Ravie Dubey plays Lakshmana. The film is produced by Namit Malhotra's Prime Focus Studios together with Yash's Monster Mind Creations and visual effects company DNEG, with music by Oscar winners A. R. Rahman and Hans Zimmer.

Ravana: villain in one telling, king in another

In the Ramayana traditionally attributed to the sage Valmiki, Ravana is the ruler of Lanka who abducts Sita and goes to war with Rama. Lanka is commonly identified with present-day Sri Lanka, although that identification has developed over centuries of literary, religious and cultural interpretation.

Sri Lankan traditions often present him differently. In some tellings he is a learned king, a scholar, a musician and a devotee of Shiva, associated with traditional medicine and with the ravanahatha, a bowed string instrument. Some communities celebrate him as a symbol of the island's ancient civilisation.

Scholar Justin W. Henry traces how that image developed in Ravana's Kingdom: The Ramayana and Sri Lankan History from Below (Oxford University Press). He describes how Ravana became an important cultural figure for parts of the Sinhala Buddhist population through a modern revival that presents him as a powerful indigenous king, and how sympathetic portrayals also appear in Sri Lankan Tamil Hindu traditions.

It is important to separate tradition from history. There is no conclusive archaeological or historical evidence that Ravana existed as a real ruler, and stories about flying machines and advanced medicine belong to folklore and mythology. Places such as Ravana Falls near Ella are linked to the epic by local tradition. For Sri Lankan viewers, Yash's portrayal therefore carries a meaning beyond that of a conventional antagonist.

A two-part film with a reported US$500 million budget

The project's cost has drawn as much attention as its box office. Producer Namit Malhotra has reportedly put the budget at about ₹4,000 crore, roughly US$500 million or AED1.84 billion, for the two-part film. In August 2026, Yash said that figure is not the cost of one film: it covers both parts and includes release and promotion.

Part One is meant to establish the story and characters before Part Two, which is scheduled for Diwali 2027. Box office receipts are not the same as producer profit, because cinemas and distributors take a share, and streaming and other rights will also affect returns.

In UAE cinemas

The film is showing across the UAE in Hindi, Tamil, Telugu and Malayalam, and in an English version, according to cinema listings reported by Gulf News. Khaleej Times reported in September that the international English cut would drop the songs and trim scenes, running about 30 minutes shorter than the Hindi version, though the makers had not confirmed the details. Check your cinema's listing for exact runtimes.

No UAE-specific box office figure has been published so far.

What comes next

Opening-day records are only the start. Diwali falls on Sunday 8 November, within the film's opening weekend, and Sacnilk notes that earlier pre-Diwali releases such as Housefull 4 and Krrish 3 grew after the festival. With such a large budget and a planned sequel, word of mouth over the coming week will matter more than the first day.

The overseas and worldwide numbers above are provisional and may change as international markets report.

The United States has issued a fresh security alert for its citizens across the Middle East, warning of an increased threat of armed attacks by Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi movement and alleged Iranian efforts to target US government officials. The alert was issued by the US Mission to the UAE on Saturday 7 November 2026, according to Gulf News. It also tells Americans to prepare for possible flight cancellations, airspace closures and other travel disruptions.

The alert is addressed to American citizens across the region. It does not name a specific threat to Dubai or any other location in the UAE, and it does not say an attack has taken place in the country.

What the alert says

The US Mission told Americans in the Middle East to exercise heightened vigilance because of two concerns: armed attacks by Iranian-supported Houthis, and Iranian efforts to target US government officials in the region. It also urged them to be ready for changes to air travel.

Gulf News notes that the alert follows earlier US warnings about Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia, including civilian airports and critical infrastructure, which Washington said caused casualties and significant travel disruption. In a 20 September alert, the US Mission said the conflict had the potential to escalate rapidly and that Iran and groups aligned with it could target other US interests abroad, including businesses and institutions.

Is Dubai under an immediate threat?

Nothing in the alert says so. It is a regional precautionary notice, part of a series of warnings tied to the wider conflict involving Iran, Israel and the United States in 2026. The UAE is already at Level 3 ("Reconsider Travel") on the US State Department's scale, and reports say the advisory was renewed in late October with the level unchanged.

A foreign government's security alert should be taken seriously, but it is not the same as a confirmed local emergency. UAE residents should rely on announcements from UAE authorities for local safety guidance. At the time of writing, no UAE announcement of airport closures or new security measures had been reported in the coverage reviewed for this article.

What it could mean for flights

The Gulf is a major aviation corridor linking Europe, Asia, Africa and the Americas, and Dubai and Abu Dhabi airports are key connection points. When regional conflicts lead to airspace restrictions, airlines can reroute, delay or cancel services. The US Mission's warning reflects that risk, but it is a warning about possible disruption, not a report that Dubai's airports are affected.

What residents and travellers can do

  • Check your flight directly. Confirm status with your airline and the airport before heading out.
  • Follow official channels. Rely on UAE government and aviation authority announcements rather than social media rumours.
  • Review your own government's advice. US citizens can enrol in the State Department's Smart Traveler Enrollment Program (STEP) to receive embassy alerts. Other nationals can check their own embassy or travel advisory service.
  • Keep arrangements flexible. Check airline change policies and travel insurance terms if you have international trips planned.

Why it matters for Dubai

Dubai relies on dependable international connectivity for tourism, trade and business travel. Regional security headlines can affect traveller confidence even when local operations continue as normal. Possible knock-on effects include higher travel costs, rerouted cargo and changed corporate travel plans, but none of these has been confirmed as a result of the 7 November alert.

Staying informed

The practical message is preparedness rather than alarm. Regional developments can change quickly, so check official updates and confirm travel plans before departure.

Dubai is one of the world's most closely watched property markets, drawing residents, overseas investors and institutional capital. Its appeal rests on a favourable personal tax environment, international connectivity, a large expatriate population and a dedicated regulatory framework.

But record headlines are not a guide to individual returns. Dubai has cycles, supply risks and large differences between neighbourhoods, and 2026 has brought a slowdown. This guide sets out the data, how Dubai compares with other global cities, and what to check before buying.

The 2025 numbers

According to Dubai government figures, the emirate recorded more than 270,000 real estate transactions worth AED917 billion in 2025, up 20% year on year. Investment transactions exceeded AED680 billion across 258,600 deals. The investor base grew to about 193,100, including roughly 129,600 new investors.

The rental market was also active. Dubai Land Department data shows 1.38 million registered tenancy contracts worth AED126.4 billion in 2025, with volume up 6% and value up 17%. More than 513,000 contracts were new tenancies, up 10%.

These are completed-year statistics. They show a broad market, but they do not guarantee that any single apartment, villa or off-plan project will appreciate.

The 2026 picture: a market cooling

The picture has changed this year. UBS's 2026 Global Real Estate Bubble Index scores Dubai at 1.16 (up from 1.09), ranking it fourth of 23 cities in the "elevated risk" category. UBS says inflation-adjusted prices rose only 0.4% annually in the second quarter while real rents fell 4%, and that uncertainty over inflows of high earners during the Iran conflict is expected to weigh on the premium segment.

UBS also finds Dubai relatively affordable and says high rents still favour buying over renting. The index does not predict whether or when a correction will occur. Savills' H1 2026 research forecasts prime values in Dubai falling around 10% in the second half of 2026, the outlier among the 30 cities it tracks, citing oversupply and geopolitical uncertainty. That is a forecast for the prime segment, not an observed fall everywhere. Emaar founder Mohamed Alabbar has said he expects an adjustment of 5% to 10%, with "a nice balance" in 2027.

How Dubai compares with other cities

Prestige is not the right yardstick. The useful questions are how much capital is needed, what rent a property can generate, what ownership costs, and how easily an overseas buyer can purchase.

On affordability, UBS says a skilled service worker needs about five years of income to buy a 60 sq m apartment near the centre of Dubai, compared with 11 years in London and 15 in Hong Kong.

Factor Dubai London New York Singapore Hong Kong
Foreign ownership Designated freehold areas Generally available Generally available Available, with additional buyer duties Generally available
Personal tax on rent No UAE personal income tax; home-country tax may apply Taxable Taxable Taxable Taxable
Annual property tax No general residential property tax; service charges apply Council tax and other charges Property tax Annual property tax Rates and government rent
Entry costs DLD transfer fee and other costs Stamp duty, including surcharges Transfer taxes and closing costs High additional duty for many foreign buyers Stamp duty and other costs

This is an indicative structural comparison, not a tax calculation. Rules depend on nationality, residency, ownership structure and financing. Dubai's lack of personal income tax does not exempt investors from tax in their country of residence.

London and New York offer deep, mature markets with long records, but higher taxes and ownership costs for many investors. Singapore is tightly regulated and supply-constrained, with extra duties for foreign buyers. Hong Kong is high-density and expensive per square foot. Dubai's case is a lower entry barrier, more property types and tax advantages, offset by a younger, supply-driven market with greater exposure to sentiment and construction cycles.

What attracts investors

  • Tax: the UAE has no personal income tax, so rental income received by an individual is generally not taxed there. Company ownership, corporate tax, VAT and home-country rules may apply.
  • Demand: Dubai's role as a business and travel hub supports demand from employees, families, entrepreneurs and visitors.
  • Strategies: long-term rental, short-term rental (subject to licensing), capital appreciation, off-plan, luxury and commercial property each carry a different risk profile.
  • Residency: Dubai Land Department materials describe a renewable 10-year residence route for investors holding property worth at least AED2 million. Sources conflict on how mortgaged, off-plan or multiple properties count, and the rules appear to be changing in 2026, so verify with DLD or the federal authorities before buying.
  • Strategy: the Dubai Economic Agenda D33 and Dubai Real Estate Sector Strategy 2033 set ambitions, including AED1 trillion in annual transactions. They are not guaranteed returns.

Regulation and safeguards

Foreign nationals can own property in designated freehold areas under Dubai Law No. 7 of 2006, registered with the Dubai Land Department (DLD). The DLD says transactions not registered in its records are not valid, so insist on official documentation.

Off-plan developers must hold buyer payments in project-specific escrow accounts, and a portion is retained for a period after completion to cover defects. Sources differ on the amount (reported at 5% to 10% for about a year), so check the project's escrow agreement. Escrow protects payments but does not remove delivery, price or developer risk.

Reading the data

Different tools serve different purposes. DLD's open data and Dubai REST are the official records for registered transactions, rental indices and service charges. Analytics platforms such as DXBinteract, Property Monitor and REIDIN add area comparisons and trends. Portals such as Bayut, Property Finder and Dubizzle show asking prices, which are a lead and not proof of value.

A practical workflow is to find properties on the portals, compare asking prices with completed transactions, check rents and service charges, then verify the developer, project registration, escrow arrangements and broker through official DLD services.

Yields: gross versus net

Gross yield is annual rent divided by purchase price. An apartment bought for AED1.5 million and let for AED105,000 a year has a gross yield of 7%, or AED8,750 a month.

That figure excludes service charges, maintenance, vacancy, management fees, financing, acquisition costs and eventual selling costs. Net yield, which subtracts operating costs and divides by total investment cost, is the figure that matters. Advertised yields can rest on optimistic rents, so compare registered leases, competing listings and actual service charges.

Risks

  • Supply: many similar units arriving in one community can pressure rents and prices.
  • Price corrections: the 2026 forecasts above show prices do not rise every year.
  • Off-plan delivery: delays, changes in market conditions and specification differences.
  • Costs: high service charges and poor maintenance cut net returns.
  • Liquidity: a quick sale can mean a discount, especially in a slowdown.
  • Currency: the dirham is pegged to the US dollar, so investors in other currencies keep exchange-rate exposure.

A due-diligence checklist

  • Is the property in a designated ownership area, and is the developer and project registered?
  • If off-plan, is there a project escrow account and a delivery record?
  • What do completed sales and registered leases support, not just listings?
  • What are the service charges and total acquisition costs?
  • How much comparable supply is available and coming?
  • Can you hold through falling prices or vacancy?

If an investment only works under an optimistic resale price or maximum rent, it is not robust.

Conclusion

Dubai has established itself as a serious global property market, with scale, tax advantages, data access and a regulated framework. But in 2026 the market is in a more demanding phase, with cooling growth, rising supply and geopolitical uncertainty. The best investment is the property whose location, price, rent, building quality and costs make sense independently of the marketing. This article is not financial or legal advice.

articles.summaryDescription: Dubai recorded AED917 billion in real estate transactions in 2025, up 20%, but price growth has cooled in 2026 amid the Iran conflict and rising supply. UBS rates the city at elevated bubble risk yet among the more affordable major markets, while Savills forecasts a roughly 10% fall in prime values in the second half of 2026. For investors the decision comes down to net yield, supply, regulation and tax, not citywide headlines.

faqs.q: How big was Dubai's property market in 2025?
faqs.a: Dubai recorded more than 270,000 real estate transactions worth AED917 billion in 2025, up 20% on the year, according to the Dubai government. The investor base reached about 193,100, including roughly 129,600 new investors.

faqs.q: Is the Dubai property market still rising in 2026?
faqs.a: Growth has slowed. UBS reported that inflation-adjusted prices rose only 0.4% annually in the second quarter while real rents fell 4%, and Savills forecasts prime values falling around 10% in the second half of 2026.

faqs.q: How does Dubai compare with London, New York, Singapore and Hong Kong?
faqs.a: UBS says a skilled service worker needs about five years of income to buy a 60 sq m central apartment in Dubai, versus 11 in London and 15 in Hong Kong. Tax and ownership rules also differ, so investors should compare net returns after all costs.

faqs.q: Is Dubai rental income tax-free?
faqs.a: The UAE has no personal income tax for individuals, so rental income received personally is generally not taxed there. Companies may face corporate tax, and investors may owe tax in their home country.

faqs.q: What protections exist for off-plan buyers?
faqs.a: Developers selling off-plan must use project-specific escrow accounts, and the Dubai Land Department says unregistered transactions are not valid. These safeguards reduce but do not remove delivery, price and developer risk.

Hussain Sajwani, the Emirati founder of DAMAC Properties, is estimated by Forbes to be worth about $15.3 billion. His wealth is tied mainly to Dubai luxury real estate, with newer interests in branded residences, AI investments and data-centre infrastructure.

Net worth figures are estimates and change with markets, and the $15.3 billion figure could not be checked against Forbes' live profile for 14 November. His pledged $20 billion for US data centres is a commitment, not confirmed spending.

Who is Hussain Sajwani?

Sajwani is the founder and chairman of DAMAC Group. DAMAC Properties is one of Dubai's largest private developers, with Amira Sajwani as managing director. The group's investment arm, DAMAC Capital, holds stakes in companies including SpaceX, Stripe, Anthropic, xAI and Mistral, according to Sajwani's own profile.

Hussain Sajwani's net worth in 2026

Forbes puts his net worth at $15.3 billion as of 2026, equal to roughly AED 56 billion at the dirham's fixed peg. The estimate has risen sharply. Forbes put it at $10.2 billion in 2025, up from $5.1 billion in 2024, and $2.7 billion in 2022. The 2025 estimate placed him at the top of Forbes' UAE list.

From catering to DAMAC Properties

Sajwani began in food services, supplying the US military and construction group Bechtel. Forbes Middle East says he launched his first business during the early 1980s oil crash. He still owns the food-service firm, according to Forbes Middle East's 2017 profile.

In 2001, after Dubai allowed foreigners to own property, he moved into real estate and sold units in a residential building in under six months. He founded DAMAC Properties in 2002.

DAMAC's sales: 2025 and 2026

DAMAC recorded Dh36 billion in sales in 2025. That is about $9.8 billion, and it included Dh11 billion in five hours at the November launch of DAMAC Islands 2. The 2024 DAMAC Islands launch generated over Dh10.2 billion in under 24 hours and was recognised by Guinness World Records.

Context matters. DXBinteract data put DAMAC second by sales value in 2025 (AED 35.9 billion) behind Emaar (AED 65.8 billion), and second by transaction count behind Binghatti. DAMAC says it has delivered 50,000 units, with over 54,000 more under construction. In March 2026 it reported AED 3.12 billion in sales across 1,106 transactions. Sales figures measure transaction value, not profit.

Branded residences and the Trump connection

DAMAC markets properties through global brands. Analysts at GRI Institute link its branded partnerships to Cavalli, Versace, Trump and Chelsea. In 2025 it launched Chelsea Residences with Chelsea Football Club.

DAMAC teamed up with Donald Trump in 2013 to develop two Trump-branded golf courses in Dubai. AP described Sajwani as a close business partner of the Trump family, and reported that discussions about a promised $2 billion in deals after Trump's 2016 win never materialised.

Data centres and AI investments

On 7 January 2025, Donald Trump, then president-elect, announced at Mar-a-Lago that Sajwani would invest $20 billion in US data centres. Sajwani said DAMAC planned to invest $20 billion, and more if market opportunities allowed. The plan runs through EDGNEX, a DAMAC unit, with sites in Texas, Arizona, Oklahoma, Louisiana, Ohio, Illinois, Michigan and Indiana.

AP noted the pledge could represent about 2% of expected US data-centre investment, and that it also showed wealthy investors close to Trump could profit from the relationship. The pledge is an announced commitment. No sources reviewed confirm how much has been spent.

On AI, DAMAC's family office invested about $50 million in Anthropic by acquiring a stake from FTX's bankrupt estate, and made undisclosed investments in xAI and Mistral. DAMAC Capital also announced returns on SpaceX and Stripe investments in August 2024.

Philanthropy

Sajwani backs education through the Hussain Sajwani – DAMAC Foundation, including the Dubai Schools Project, which provides scholarships to UAE national children, and the One Million Arab Coders initiative.

What to watch

  • How much of the $20 billion US data-centre commitment is built.
  • DAMAC's 2026 sales against its 2025 total.
  • Future updates to Forbes' net worth estimate.

Analysis

This section is analysis, not reporting.

Sajwani's strategy relies on two bets: that branded luxury property keeps drawing global buyers to Dubai, and that AI infrastructure will reward developers who can build at scale. Both are cyclical, and data centres need large capital, power supply and long-term customers. The Trump-linked announcements raise his profile, but sceptics note that pledges of this kind have not always been delivered in full.

Updated November 2026 | Dubaiography Business & Creative Industry Guide

Dubai is one of the Middle East's main centres for creative businesses, from global advertising networks to independent branding consultancies and digital experience studios. This Dubaiography guide profiles 10 creative agencies in Dubai worth considering in 2026, with their specialisations, recognition and the kinds of business each suits.

This is a curated editorial guide, not a statistically weighted ranking. Dubaiography is a Darwin Corp product, and Darwin Corp is listed first as the publisher's own studio. That placement is not a claim that it holds the highest independently verified industry ranking. The "best for" notes are editorial judgements.

Why choosing a creative agency in Dubai is harder than it looks

Finding the best creative agency in Dubai involves more than choosing a company that can produce attractive designs or advertising campaigns. Businesses increasingly need strategic brand positioning, professional website development, intuitive user experiences, visual storytelling and digital platforms that reach audiences across international markets.

As the city attracts international companies, entrepreneurs and ambitious brands, demand for sophisticated creative services has grown with it. The selection below includes Dubai-based independent studios, internationally recognised advertising networks and specialist branding consultancies.

How we selected these creative agencies

Not every creative agency delivers the same services. Some specialise in advertising and campaign strategy. Others concentrate on branding, digital product design, website development or high-end visual production. For this guide, we considered:

  • Creative capabilities: the breadth and specialisation of each agency's creative services.
  • Branding and design expertise: capabilities in brand strategy, identity and visual communication.
  • Digital experience capabilities: website design, UI/UX, digital platforms and technology integration.
  • Industry presence: publicly documented work, professional recognition and market activity.
  • Business suitability: the types of clients and project requirements each agency is positioned to serve.
  • International capabilities: the ability to support regional or global business requirements.

The agencies serve different markets and should not be treated as directly interchangeable.

Top 10 creative agencies in Dubai at a glance

Agency Primary specialisation Best suited for
1. Darwin Corp Branding, UI/UX, interactive websites and digital experiences Businesses seeking premium digital design and international remote collaboration
2. Impact BBDO Creative advertising and brand campaigns Major brands and large-scale campaigns
3. FP7 McCann Integrated advertising and brand communications Regional and multinational advertisers
4. VML Digital experiences, creativity and commerce Enterprise digital transformation
5. Saatchi & Saatchi Middle East Brand storytelling and advertising Consumer brands and integrated campaigns
6. ASTUDIO Luxury branding and visual production Luxury, hospitality and lifestyle brands
